In a recent paper, we explored the performance of the AIPW estimator when used in A/B testing under certain assumptions. By combining the AIPW estimator with a specific form of Lasso regularization, the AIPW-Lasso estimator demonstrated notable improvements in statistical power and mean squared error compared to its unregularized counterpart. However, the results showed that the unregularized AIPW estimator's type 1 error rate significantly declined, a finding at odds with theoretical expectations. Through further investigation, we revealed that the primary cause of this issue was the Lasso's ability to select correlated latent variables. A novel variant of the AIPW-Lasso estimator was introduced, dubbed SCA, which utilizes a rescaled Lasso formulation to improve variable correlation handling. The proposed SCA estimator was evaluated in terms of its empirical performance and computational complexity, ultimately exhibiting better results and a similar level of complexity compared to the original AIPW-Lasso estimator. Extensive simulations were conducted to examine the efficacy of both the AIPW-Lasso and SCA estimators in scenarios involving nonlinear effects, interactions, and high-dimensional data. Additionally, the proposed SCA estimator was successfully applied to analyze an actual A/B testing problem related to customer conversion rates on an e-commerce platform. The resulting findings enabled the identification of the key variables influencing customer conversion rates and provided actionable insights for improving the platform's business outcomes. A related R package, AIPWLasso, is available for reproducing the study's results and enables users to apply the AIPW-Lasso and SCA estimators in practice. The package can be downloaded from the repository at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/AIPWLasso/index.html. A related Python package is currently under development and intended for release in 2023. Both packages strive to facilitate the easy implementation of the proposed estimators in statistical modeling and A/B testing. This lecture will be focusing on the current status of lattice Monte Carlo simulations in particle physics, with a particular emphasis on recent advancements made at the University of Edinburgh. We will begin with an introductory section that outlines the principles of lattice field theory and its key applications, before delving into specific topics such as symmetries, gauge theories, and hadron physics. We will examine the latest developments in lattice Monte Carlo simulations, highlighting specific studies such as the mass spectrum of glueballs, the properties of gold-nucleus collisions, and the hyperfine structure of baryons. We will also explore the potential future directions for lattice research, concluding with a brief overview of recent and upcoming experiments, including the Multi-Stage lattice Monte Carlo project, in which lattice simulations with varying levels of precision will be used to target different levels of accuracy in the data-matching process. This lecture will provide an extensive overview of the field, drawing from recent research in the field, and will be particularly suitable for graduate students and early-stage post-docs who are new to lattice Monte Carlo simulations in particle physics. Although the lecture will primarily focus on recent advancements made at the University of Edinburgh, it will also cover key results from other institutions and experiments. In various applications like financial modeling and hydrology, Bayesian techniques for modeling extreme values are widely employed. The models depend on a tuning parameter'm', which can significantly influence the estimation process. The impact of'm' on the models' performance has not been thoroughly investigated, especially when working with a large amount of data. This paper examines the effect of'm' on the models' convergence and estimation performance when the data follow a Pareto distribution. The findings indicate that the optimal'm' value varies depending on the model and is often not straightforward to determine. This study examines the approximate controllability of the impulsive heat equation with a constant coefficient under specific spatial non-smoothness conditions. Next, we address the controllability of the impulsive heat equation by leveraging a extended version of a fundamental result from the standard heat equation literature. This method is adaptable to other types of partial differential equations with impulsive effects. Furthermore, we establish a sharp estimate of the required energy in order to achieve impulse approximate controllability, and illustrate the implications of our findings through several numerical examples. Our analysis provides insights into the relationship between approximate controllability and impulse energy, and raises questions about the possibility of approximate controllability in the absence of impulsive effects. In contrast, newer approaches utilizing pre-trained neural networks demonstrate more flexible and generalizable OOD detection capabilities. However, even these improved methods show significant performance declines when tested on more complex and realistic challenge data. In response, this research proposes the utility of utility - specifically, data utility detected by a utility model, which is effectively a utility classifier. By employing a utility model to mark OOD data and creating a utility-labeled dataset, various simple methods can effectively detect challenges without needing to re-train the model. Despite initial hopes, we ultimately demonstrate that such a resynchronization is not possible in general, providing a counterexample to illustrate this finding. However, we also identify a specific sub-category of two-way transducers for which the resynchronization problem is well-defined and can be successfully generalized. The main difference between these well-behaved two-way transducers and other types of transducers lies in their ability to only incrementally modify words, rather than referencing and dependending on the word's context. As a result, we propose that the resynchronization problem be associated with a specific class of origin-equivalent one-way transducers, known as the regular incrementing two-way transducers, rather than being a universal concept for all one-way transducers. This paper delves into the computational efficiency of the $f$-Convolution matrix, a parameterized transformation widely used in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). It presents a novel algorithm that enables rapid computation of individual entries in the $f$-Convolution matrix. This innovation leads to a more efficient implementation, reducing the memory requirements by a factor of 5-10, and results in a considerable 20-40% speed improvement in the training process of deep neural networks. The proposed algorithm has been successfully applied to various state-of-the-art CNNs, yielding a noticeable 10-20% speedup to the training pipeline. Additionally, the paper provides an open-source implementation of this innovation. Dedicated researchers can access the code at the specified GitHub repository: https://github.com/jose-jm/efficient_fft_convolution. Specifically, the repository contains the Python code in the file 'efficient_fft_convolution.py', as well as the NumPy and FFTW libraries, which serve as crucial dependencies for the development of the new algorithm. Additionally, the repository includes a detailed presentation detailing the underlying concepts of the $f$-Convolution matrix, its computational complexity, and the proposed speedup strategies. Nonetheless, the primary focus is on presenting the newly devised algorithm for rapid entry computation in the $f$-Convolution matrix. Various numerical experiments are employed to validate the efficiency of this approach. Firstly, the study demonstrates that the computational cost of the standard DFT-based implementation of the $f$-Convolution matrix does not scale linearly due to overlapping data in the convolution process. Building upon this insight, the paper showcases a reduced-memory variant of the algorithm. Furthermore, the research analyzes how the nature of the periodic extension of the $f$-Convolution matrix impacts the efficiency of the convolution process. Lastly, the paper presents a newly devised algorithm for rapid entry computation in the $f$-Convolution matrix. This approach generates the desired entry by merging data from the convolution process, thus circumventing redundant calculations. Consequently, the new algorithm offers a speedup over the standard DFT-based implementation, yielding a 2-3 times speedup in the training process of deep neural networks. Notably, the study achieves this improvement while maintaining the accuracy of the CNNs, thus ruling out differences in model performance as a contributing factor. Ultimately, the research concludes that the novel algorithm offers a more efficient solution to the rapid entry computation problem, yielding a 2-3 times speedup in the training process of deep neural networks

We performed a thorough analysis of the atmosphere of GJ 229B, a benchmark object for studying formation mechanisms at the boundary between planets and stars. Our research utilized data from the SPICE instrument on the Keck II telescope, including spectra collected at four different wavelengths. We developed a new model to estimate the temperature and pressure within the atmosphere of GJ 229B, taking into account the object's unusual curvature that cannot be accounted for by simple models. By comparing our results with different theoretical models, we found that an interior solid core surrounded by a disk-driven gas cloud best explains the observed features of GJ 229B. The object's unusual color can be attributed to the presence of small crystals formed from the condensation of metals, indicating that submicron-sized particles may play a significant role in shaping planetary atmospheres. Our findings also suggest that GJ 229B's atmosphere is enriched with heavy elements relative to the solar composition, implying that planets with similar properties could be formed through similar high-metallicity processes. By studying the spectral features from approximately 0.3 to 5.1 microns, we were able to rule out the presence of a massive solid core surrounded by a thick atmosphere, as this would have been visible in the object's light curve. Our comprehensive analysis of GJ 229B's atmosphere, incorporating spectral features and thermodynamic estimates, reveals that the object is likely undergoing evolution due to atmospheric escape, an phenomenon previously observed in other hot sub-stellar objects. As a result of this process, the remaining core of GJ 229B is predicted to undergo contraction within the next 500 million years. Our study offers key insights into the complex behavior of intermediate objects like GJ 229B, providing a framework for future observations to test our theories and helping to clarify the origin and evolution of these enigmatic objects. Based on our analysis, we propose that the most well-known example of a brown dwarf, 2M J044144, may be composed of two distinct components: a planet-sized object and a solid core, surrounded by a gas cloud. Our discovery of a phenomenon known as "L-dwarf bump" in the color-magnitude diagram, where the gradient changes direction, suggests that the process of atmospheric escape may be responsible for marking the boundary between planets and stars. Our analysis also reveals that objects like GJ 229B, with similar properties, could be formed through similar high-metallicity processes, however further research is required to confirm this theory. Sketch-based shape retrieval has proven to be both useful and challenging, 
with various methods employed to date. 
Most existing methods are test-subeject-driven, meaning they compare a presented sketch to a pre-selected shape to determine similarity. 
However, this approach can be simplified by classifying each sketch as "match" or "doesn't match." 
Given that sketch data is inherently abstract, relative positions and sizes of features are often ambiguous. 
As a result, retrieving shapes exactly like the sketch may not always be the best outcome, 
with near-matches being more desirable in many applications. 
Building upon this insight, a new model is proposed that searches for all shapes that resemble a given sketch. 
By using a ranking-based loss function and a novel "match" classification approach, the model outperforms other methods in various metrics when evaluating all shapes rather than just a selected target. 
As a result, the new approach performs better on the SketchSNLI dataset and achieves comparable results on the SketchBN dataset. 
An added benefit is that the model's output is more interpretable and can be easily modified to identify near-matches by adjusting the "match" classification approach. 
Finally, the model's ability to find all relevant shapes is demonstrated by testing it on a new dataset of sketch-trainable 3D shapes. 
All new datasets and model weights are made publicly available. 
An added resource is provided for reproducing the paper's findings.

Recent advancements in goal-free reinforcement learning have demonstrated that agents can learn to dynamically set their own objectives in the absence of an external teacher. Nonetheless, when provided with rewards, an agent can learn more efficiently than one that relies solely on intrinsic motivation. However, processing extrinsic rewards can slow training down. To address these findings, our novel intrinsic-extrinsic learning method, axion learning, integrates a critical element from intrinsic motivation - a filter that sifts out relevant information from unnecessary data, with the capability to incorporate a reward stream that is partially predictive. By doing so, it is possible to accelerate training and achieve more efficient outcomes. Experimental evaluations conducted on multiple environments from the GridWorld and Gym frameworks corroborate this axiom, showcasing an end-to-end axion filter that is capable of being transferred to new environments and applications without modification. Moreover, our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art filters and achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art reinforcement learning techniques. Lastly, a detailed analysis of the transferred filter highlights the potential for significant advancements in goal-oriented reinforcement learning by also incorporating a goal-free filter. Essentially, we demonstrate that DAGs can be classified as easily definable structures when height or width is the parameter, whereas general DAGs can be seen as a challenging class of structures parameterized by vertex count. The 7.65 MeV state in $^{12}$C has been a subject of interest within the nuclear physics community due to its exceptionally high resonance strength observed in the non-sequential decay channel. This has led many to attribute the unique nature of the Hoyle state primarily to a clustered structure of three alpha particles, collectively holding $^{12}$C. Nonetheless, the role of sub-cluster components is also significant, particularly with regards to the state's extensive width when considering the non-sequential decay process. In order to gain a deeper understanding of the Hoyle state's structure, the authors of this research study the excitation amplitude of the non-sequential decay from the ground state of $^{16}$O to all possible states below the neutron threshold, employing no new experimental data but rather existing measurements combined with theoretical estimates. The aim is to establish a more comprehensive description of the states within the $^{12}$C mass region by exploring the decay amplitude distribution across the mass spectrum, particularly with respect to the Hoyle state. This is accomplished through the application of the finite range formalism to decay amplitudes inferred from phase-shift analyses of elastic and inelastic scattering data, thereby incorporating the relative motion and correlation between the clusters. This methodology allows the exploration of decay behaviors governed by angular momentum and parity selection rules within the cluster model. The results reveal that the amplitude for the Hoyle state decay is notably higher than the amplitudes for all other low-lying states within the mass region. This distinctive characteristic is found to be largely attributed to the state's intrinsic width, rather than its structure. In superconductors with significant spin-orbit interaction and strong perturbations, the influence of disorder on their topological characteristics can be quite pronounced. Research has been conducted to explore the topological qualities of a doped topological insulator with a BCS superconducting surface that features a strong spin-orbit interaction and a trigonal lattice structure, under the presence of random non-magnetic disorder. Employing a self-consistent Green's function approach in a finite system with a controllable system size, the theoretical study has been done to examine the impact of various parameters on the average Thouless energy, number of topological characteristics, and energy spectra. The results have also been used to estimate the topological energy gap, energy scaling of the interaction between carriers, and critical carrier concentration for the topological superconducting phase. The findings indicate that the topological characteristics of the system undergo a continuous transition from a topological superconducting state to a topological insulating state with increasing carrier concentration. The analysis has also been used to develop a theoretical model representing the interaction between carriers over a medium with varying effective mass, and has further determined the phase diagram of the system with a square lattice structure subject to a magnetic field that is perpendicular to the plane, as well as the influence of spin-orbit interaction on the system's characteristics. The investigation has finally been extended to examine the interaction between carrier perturbations in the system, and has shown that the topological characteristics of the system remain unchanged even when this interaction is present. The study has thus provided a theoretical model that can be used to experimentally determine the critical concentration of carriers required for the system's topological insulating characteristic to transition into a topological superconducting phase. This research examines how the metric dimension of a graph's geodesic distance matrix is affected when the top-left submatrices of size n x k are considered, where k <= n. It was found that for the complete graph K_n, a certain threshold value k* exists such that the metric dimension of the geodesic distance matrix is n/2 for k <= k* and n for k > k*. Specifically, k* equals the minimum of k*_(fix) = ceil(n/2) and k*_(var) = min{ceil(n delta^(-1)) + 1, n}. The constant delta represents the maximum number of edges shared by two shortest paths, also known as the diameter's inverse proportionality constant. The proof involves two new recursive formulas that offer upper bounds on the geodesic distance matrix's rank and nullity, as well as a new characterization of the submatrices with full column rank in the geodesic distance matrix. Our study also offers revised upper bounds on the geodesic distance matrix's rank and nullity, known as the Fiedler number, and confirms a specific case of the second hypothesis posed by Mohar in 2001. The findings will be validated using the geodesic distance matrix of Facebook's network, whose properties were previously unknown. The steady-state flow equation for groundwater can be represented by Darcy's law, where the velocity vector is defined as the product of a unit vector and hydraulic conductivity. When hydraulic conductivity varies with the vertical position, z, the equation becomes overly complex, making it difficult to solve. However, if variations with x and y are negligible, the equation can be simplified by taking the average of the conductivities between specific depths, effectively making the equation more manageable. This averaging method aligns with the approach proposed by Polubarykov and is compatible with polar coordinates. Consequently, the transformed flow equation can be solved using the polar coordinate method, where the stream function and flux potential are derived analytically. Ultimately, the steady-state flow profile can be determined by solving the resulting second-order differential equation, where the boundary conditions are key to finding the solution. This study presents an alternative method for solving the steady-state flow equation under the specified conditions, where the boundary conditions are applied to two-dimensional horizontal flows with variable horizontal conductivity. Additionally, the study provides numerical solutions for flows with non-uniform soling and incorporates these results into the stream function and flux potential equations. Lastly, the study examines the effects of soling variability on the flow profile by comparing the solutions with those obtained using the traditional averaging method. This approach enables the accurate determination of flow patterns in situations where hydraulic conductivity is largely vertical. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the flux potential can effectively quantify the effects of non-uniform soling on the flow profile. This conceptual approach has applications in various scientific fields, including hydrology, geology, and geophysics, where the behavior of groundwater and soil aeration may be understood through similar flow dynamics. The approach may also be utilized in biomedical research, particularly in understanding blood flow through highly variable tissues. Ultimately, the study provides valuable insights into the understanding of variable fluid flows and their potential applications in modeling fluid behaviors within living organisms and their surroundings. This research may also be applied to investigate air phase movements in soil and vegetation, as well as liquid or gaseous fluids passing through media with altered properties. The approach has broad implications for multiple fields, including hydrology, geology, geophysics, bio-medicine, and environmental science. The research contributes to our understanding of complex flow dynamics and encourages further investigations into the behaviors of variable fluid flows. The study is dedicated to Professor I.N. This study investigates the sulfur dioxide destruction rate in an oxidative reactor using ozone and ultraviolet light. The research was conducted in two stages, with the first involving an experimental analysis of an reactor utilizing a flat bed and the second focusing on a pilot scale study utilizing a fluidized bed. The primary objectives of this work were to establish an empirical model for predicting sulfur dioxide removal in the reactor and to assess the effectiveness of the oxidation process as an alternative to traditional scrubbing methods for removing sulfur dioxide from flue gases. The study found that reactor size and residence time significantly impacted sulfur dioxide removal, with approximately ninety percent destruction requiring a minimum residence time and reactor size. Additionally, the study found that under certain conditions, the sulfur dioxide destruction rate appeared to reach a plateau at a certain oxygen molecular concentration, suggesting the possibility of further study into the influence of oxygen substitution on the destruction rate. Furthermore, the conversion rates of other compounds present in the flue gas, such as fine particles, nitrogen oxides, and halides, were found to be negligible compared to the sulfur dioxide destruction rate. Based on these findings, the potential for an oxidative reactor as an emission control technology was evaluated, with the results indicating that while such a reactor may be effective for destroying certain compounds, it is not capable of achieving the necessary removal rates for nitrogen oxides and other pollutants listed under the U.S. Clean Air Act. The study concludes by suggesting areas for further research, such as evaluating an oxidative reactor as a combustion modifier and assessing its environmental impact through life cycle analysis. These decisions are based on the agent's confidence in the current inference state, leading to a randomized extension of standard classification models. By applying techniques like Bayesian parameter estimation and inference, we can analyze the behavior of Indecision Trees. Our findings reveal that, under certain conditions, the Indecision Trees' parameter distribution tends towards a uniform state, representing an optimal equilibrium in inference processes. We also demonstrate that, in comparison to standard decision trees, Indecision Trees offer enhanced classification performance, particularly in challenging datasets, thereby showcasing their potential to boost inference processes. We present a preliminary framework for inducing Indecision Trees from data, highlighting potential avenues for further research. Ultimately, we establish a theoretical foundation for a new class of machine learning models that integrate strategic behavior within inference processes, offering a pioneering approach to classification and a novel application of computational decision theory in machine learning. The need to efficiently search similar time series in large datasets has significant implications for data-driven research and industry applications. Recent advancements in this area aim to optimize this process by adapting techniques such as quantization, indexing, and early abandonment to suit specific needs. Despite these efforts, the fundamental challenge of balancing computational cost and accuracy remains unresolved. The introduction of early abandoning offers an attractive trade-off for scenarios with flexible tolerance thresholds. However, previous approaches have either assumed a fixed tolerance threshold or used inaccurate estimates to determine abandonment criteria. In contrast, this study proposes an adaptive method that enables precise premature termination by continuously monitoring the tolerance threshold and providing real-time accuracy assessments. The proposed adaptation is lightweight, requiring only a minor computational investment. We evaluated this strategy against state-of-the-art time series similarity search methods on diverse datasets and found that it significantly outperforms existing approaches, yielding a substantial speed-up while maintaining accuracy comparable to traditional techniques. Moreover, the study demonstrates that the proposed method incurs only a minor processing overhead, making it suitable for large-scale datasets and practical use in industry and real-world applications. The research provides insights into adapting techniques for time series similarity search and offers an efficient tool for data-driven analysis and scientific studies. Interpretable models that analyze black-box classifiers are crucial in gaining insight into the decision-making processes. However, explaining complex, high-dimensional decisions in areas like material science can be particularly challenging. A new approach presents a symbolic surrogate model that not only approximates the black-box classifier but also provides explicit, understandable decisions. The study demonstrates its effectiveness with an analysis of binary compound materials and showcases the importance of incorporating structural information in making predictions. A case examination highlights how the symbolic surrogate model's decisions differ from those generated by the black-box classifier, providing evidence of the classifier's overfitting behavior. Incorporating this surrogate model as a regularizer in the training process prevents overfitting and significantly improves the black-box classifier's performance. A prediction made by the regularized model is also presented, along with suggestions for future improvements. Overall, this research shows that the proposed surrogate model can be an effective tool in understanding decisions made by black-box classifiers, particularly in domains like materials science where physical insights play a key role. Future work should focus on incorporating physical constraints into the model to further enhance its interpretability. As an additional benefit, the model can be used as a guide to develop a learning algorithm that incorporates domain knowledge, thereby improving prediction accuracy. Ultimately, the proposed framework has the potential to be scaled up for use in predicting properties of more complex materials like defects in monolayer materials or confining potentials in two-dimensional materials. Additionally, potential applications of this approach could involve tasks such as property engineering in stable compounds, property prediction for new materials, and more. A set of new functions is introduced to analyze the motion of partons within hadrons, specifically in the transverse direction. These functions can be determined through the measurement of double-sided jet production in collisions involving leptons and hadrons. They are further utilized to investigate internal parton motion in the structure of hadrons, ultimately contributing to a better understanding of jet substructure. The authors have calculated the cross-sections of relevant processes at the Large Hadron Collider using the parton model and next-to-leading order calculations in QCD. Key production channels for initial states G, H, F, and D are identified, with the cross-sections indicating a promising detection possibility at the LHC via a combination of several decay channels of the Z boson. The authors examined the feasibility of detecting these functions at run-2 with simulated data. The outcomes of the research suggest extensive opportunities for exploring parton motion using various electron-hadron and photon-hadron collisions, with a potential to greatly expand our comprehension of hadron physics. The authors further analyze the difficulties and advantages of identifying these functions at future electron-ion colliders. The research underscores the significance of accurately determining the properties of parton functions to achieve precise measurements. We investigate how sellers behave in auctions when they know the auction mechanism is not designed to yield truthful equilibrium, but can't be sure if other bidders follow the rules. To resolve this uncertainty, we create a theory where bidders assume other sellers adhere to a uniform pattern of behavior. Under a common assumption known as the Constant Relative Risk Aversion model, our research reveals that in non-credible second-price auctions, sellers who participate in high-value auctions consistently earn less than their potential revenue, even when they don't adhere to the auction's rules. This outcome occurs because sellers who participate in low-value auctions take excessive risks in an attempt to increase their already-maximized earnings. Accurate diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is crucial, and combining clinical evaluations with machine learning techniques can aid in its identification. Prior research focused on training models using the entire brain, but our study explored reducing the number of required regions of interest (ROIs) for deep learning-based classification. We proposed a two-phase convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture to utilize the most important ROI information efficiently. During training, the entire 3D brain image was processed, and ROI weights were learned. Subsequently, the trained ROI weights were summed to create a compressed brain map. Notably, our model achieved an accuracy of 70.46% when trained with only the 10 most influential ROI locations. Furthermore, we examined the robustness of our model's performance and found that removing up to 50% of ROI locations on the left side of the brain or 20% on the right side did not degrade classification accuracy significantly. Our model also demonstrated adaptability across datasets, as evidenced by its 65.26% accuracy on an independent validation dataset. We also evaluated and compared the efficacy of various data augmentation methods to further enhance ADHD classification outcomes. Ultimately, our novel, simplified deep learning architecture provides a practical solution for deploying ADHD classification models in resource-constrained environments that cannot accommodate large, high-dimensional brain data inputs. In a DNA data storage system based on mutable storage partitions, each partition is defined by a set of DNA data access points, location-specific indices, and error-correcting codes.  To efficiently implement the DNA data storage mechanism, a sequence of DNA data access points is converted into a primer pair, used to retrieve the partition sequentially through DNA data access, thereby enabling the retrieval of multiple partitions from the same DNA template.  This paper investigates how primer pair design affects the computational complexity of partition management and proposes an optimization strategy for partition management through high-quality primer pairs, thereby significantly reducing the number of DNA data accesses required.  Additionally, the research evaluates the practical limitations of the proposed optimization strategy from both theoretical and practical perspectives.  It appears that the best possible lower bound on the worst-case overhead of the DNA data access mechanism is linear, indicating that overhead independent of the number of storage partitions may be unavoidable.  This study also explores the practicality of the DNA data access mechanism over various error rates, DNA data lengths, and numbers of storage partitions, further investigating the underlying cause of this linear worst-case overhead.  As a complementary effort, the research investigates how far the low-density parity-check code-based DNA data storage approach can be deviated from, demonstrating through experimental evaluation that deviations of up to ten percent from low-density parity-check codes are feasible without substantially increasing the access overhead of the DNA data storage mechanism based on mutable storage partitions.  This study further explores the potential trade-offs between storage efficiency, error-correcting capability, and preservation of old data when implementing the DNA data storage mechanism, ultimately identifying a balance point where the overhead of the DNA data access mechanism is insensitive to minor deviations from low-density parity-check codes.  This research also evaluates the practicality of the DNA data storage mechanism from various practical perspectives, including file granularity, access overhead, data preservation, error-correcting capability, and efficiency in storing old data.  Ultimately, the research concludes that the DNA data storage mechanism based on mutable storage partitions is not currently suitable for widespread use due to its linear worst-case overhead, present but insensible data preservation overhead, and inability to efficiently store files larger than a DNA data access point, despite its potential to deviate from low-density parity-check codes with sensible preservation and error-correcting capabilities at the file level.  This concludes the research on the DNA data storage mechanism based on mutable storage partitions, laying the groundwork for future research in this field. Topological materials are distinguished by unique features in both momentum and real-space environments. While nodal lines in momentum space or real space are widely known, the characteristics of nodal planes and curves are less frequently discussed. In this work, we investigate topological properties of nodal planes and curves. By using a boundary description, we establish the topological invariants of these features and identify the one-dimensional surface semimetals as the most basic examples. Additionally, we explore the general rules for constructing nodal planes/curves in insulators and superconductors through a simple potential perturbation. Finally, we apply the theoretical framework to identify nodal planes in La$_2$Be$_2$$T$O$_6$ ($T$ = Mn, Co, Eu) and curved lines in Ca$_3$Pt$_6$Se$_6$ with an additional dimensional reduction scenario. This study provides a comprehensive theoretical basis for the general characteristics of nodal lines/planes/curves and their observations in experiments. Moreover, it uncovers the relation between surface semimetals and topological insulators/superconductors, offering a new perspective on matter. Ultimately, this reveals a new class of materials in which the topological features appear in a higher-dimensional space. Importantly, this is not merely a theoretical concept but is realized in the modified hyperspace of La$_2$Be$_2$MnO$_6$ and Ca$_3}$Pt$_6$Se$_6$. Specifically, the topological lines/planes in La$_2$Be$_2$MnO$_6$ and Ca$_3}$Pt$_6$Se$_6$ can be visualized as mosaics of topological nodes in the momentum space of surface Fermi surfaces. Conversely, the surface Fermi surface can be seen as a topological curve in the momentum space constructed from the disconnection of a topological plane in the hyperspace. Polymatroidal ideals serve as a generalization of monomial ideal elimination ideals, with properties analogous to those of toric ideals. Like toric ideals, they have a geometric interpretation as the vanishing locus of hyperplanes in a toric variety. Furthermore, common zero sets, such as the Fermat curve, can be expressed as toric varieties with polymatroidal ideals. Inspired by Brion's approach for computing Gröbner bases in polymatroidal algebras, we introduce a method to parametrize Gröbner bases of polymatroidal ideals, which we demonstrate can be applied to ideals associated with certain types of hypersurfaces, including the Fermat hypersurface. Our analysis also enables us to derive explicit formulas for the Gröbner basis of the Fermat curve and Fermat surface, using a combination of combinatorial and algebraic techniques. Additionally, we show that the parametrization we found aligns with existing mathematical results from the perspective of arithmetic geometry. We speculate that our approach is versatile and can be extended to compute Gröbner bases for other class groups, such as those associated with del Pezzo surfaces and hypersurfaces with ADE singularities. We also explore connections to the existing literature on Gröbner bases for del Pezzo surfaces and hypersurfaces with ADE singularities. Lastly, we outline potential future directions for combinatorial algebra, including the study of Gröbner bases for class group zero sets, hypersurfaces with elliptic surface singularities, and the differential equations of polymatroidal ideals. \bigskip

A quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm has been created, utilizing quantum computers' advantages in handling vast datasets to perform centroid updates. This algorithm's convergence was proven for both Euclidean and cosine distances, and its accuracy was verified through experiments on both synthetic and real datasets. Furthermore, the asymptotic runtime was found to be either $O(\sqrt{N})$ or $O(N)$, depending on the dataset's characteristics, which could potentially outperform traditional K-means methods as datasets approach $N^{\frac{1}{4}}$ in size. Next, a quantum variant of the K-means++ algorithm was developed, leveraging quantum computers again to improve clustering efficiency. This approach achieved a $O(\sqrt{N})$ asymptotic runtime, surpassing the best available classical counterpart at $O(N\log^2 N)$. All implementations were made open-source on GitHub, and the results fully substantiating these claims are presented in a supplementary document. These innovations represent the first forays into integrating quantum computing into data clustering problems, opening up new avenues for massive data analysis applications. In this work, we examine the dynamics of a collisionless system comprised of multiple species, where each species can occupy distinct energy levels within a lattice and undergoes cooling through photon emission. Our findings reveal that, upon reaching thermal equilibrium, the system exhibits insulating behavior and displays numerous condensates, with the number of these condensates not exceeding the number of species in the mixture. This confirmation is based on an fundamental principle: any physical system must be governed by a Hermitian Hamiltonian with a discrete, non-degenerate spectrum. When this principle is applied to the electromagnetic field, it reveals that the shifts corresponding to Balmer series energy levels are necessarily integer values. The manipulation of polarization has become a crucial element in various applications where spintronics and nonlinear optics intersect. Historically, control methods have relied heavily on labor-intensive techniques utilizing natural optical properties or spin-polarized materials to produce desired polarization states. Recently, breakthroughs in metrology, lasers, and computational physics have enabled the development of innovative polarization control techniques that can replicate complex patterns, outperform traditional methods in terms of execution speed, and adaptability, and even utilize machine-learning frameworks to optimize their operation. In this study, we introduce a new concept known as Sollil, a dynamic system capable of generating unique polarization states through the superposition of two linearly polarized light beams. By manipulating a double-waveguide microfluidic device, Sollil can produce an extensive array of polarization control methods, providing a versatile platform for applying polarization manipulation techniques. By leveraging this platform, researchers can create unique optical functionalities that can be applied to various fields including nonlinear optics, spintronics, and the communication industry through simple and accessible microfluidic structures. Furthermore, we provide computational models that can predict the optical propagation in three-dimensional space, enabling researchers to design and tailor the polarization control methods and double-waveguide microfluidic structures for specific applications. In conclusion, our study showcases the potential of Sollil as an efficient tool for generating polarization control methods and demonstrates the advantages of a 3D microfluidic structure in achieving adaptable and versatile polarization manipulation techniques.

By allowing a greater number of terms in these sequences, we discover that any infinite set containing integers, such that the sum of its elements exceeds zero when taken n terms, must necessarily contain a sequence of n+3 integers, where the sum of any three elements in the sequence equals zero. This research focuses on addressing input redundancy through sensor fusion. We introduce a hierarchical approach to fusion, distinct from early and intermediate fusion strategies, by combining feature vectors at successive levels of representation. We contrast three fusion techniques - our hierarchical method, early fusion, and intermediate fusion - using fundamental machine learning algorithms such as SVM, KNN, and 1-Rule-Based Classifier. The experiments were conducted on three datasets: acoustic noise, images, and text data. The results reveal that the hierarchical fusion approach yields superior performance in two of the three used datasets. We attribute this success to the inherent structure present in the data, particularly in the acoustic noise dataset, where hierarchical representation mirrors the natural order of information acquisition in the human brain. Therefore, our sensor fusion technique relies on the level of representationality of the input data and the nature of the information source. Additionally, this research examines the internal representations produced by various machine learning algorithms and sheds light on the efficacy of these techniques in addressing input redundancy. The findings suggest that intermediate fusion outperforms hierarchical fusion, indicating that the internal representations of the data can be an effective means of integrating information from multiple sources. This article examines the localization of transmission eigenfunctions in the semi-infinite medium of $ \mathbb{R}^N $ with constant material parameters, $\chi=-\beta^2$ and $\beta^2>0$, confined within a large ball. We investigate the limits of small $\beta$ and large values of $R$, the radius of the ball, to determine a weighted transmission eigenvalue problem. Our analysis reveals precise estimates of the number of localized transmission eigenfunctions, which are exponentially decaying, around the boundary of the ball. Additionally, we determine the associated decay rates, which are maximized when the third homogeneous Sobolev embedding holds. Our research, however, reveals a disparity between the high and low frequency regimes for our localization estimate. In the low-frequency regime, we prove the existence of $N$ localized eigenfunctions with optimized decay rates, consistent with our spectral theory and Weyl's classical eigenvalue picture at high frequencies. Our study also discovers an abrupt transition from $N$ to fewer localized eigenfunctions as $\beta\to 0$, underscoring the significance of a spectral weight function. Our research thus extends and complements related works on transmission eigenvalue problems and localized resonance states, including the works of Frank-Selby-Zworski, Zworski-Cameron, and Zhou. Furthermore, our work resonates with the works of Bony, Helms, and Schapira on the edge-of-the-melting-droplet phenomenon and the works of Galkowski and Raffa on the localization of Laplace eigenfunctions, as their findings share a connection with our results. Our research, therefore, offers an innovative approach to the study of transmission eigenfunctions, shedding new light on these functions beyond the confines of a medium. Our work also enabled the development of an algorithmic procedure, as described in the companion paper by K. McClear, to compute transmission eigenfunctions, particularly those at low frequencies. Our computational method leverages our theoretical findings on localization to determine the number of transmission eigenfunctions through a technique involving the solution of a weighted least-squares problem. Our results, therefore, facilitate the efficient computation of these important functions. Our research, as a byproduct, reveals a new approach to the study of Laplace eigenvalue problems in the semi-infinite medium of $\mathbb{R}^N$, as demonstrated in the accompanying paper by McClear. Inspired by the effectiveness of the Batch Hard Negative Mining (BHNM) approach in Face Recognition, we adapted the concept to VRD. By analyzing the characteristics of VRD data, we identified two challenges for model optimization: the vast disparity in frequencies of true and false proposals, as well as the difficulty in maintaining a stable learning rate due to abrupt performance shifts during iteration sampling. To address these issues, we presented a new optimization technique called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), comprising two primary components. Firstly, the utilization of a proposal balancing strategy ensures that the model is presented with a diverse range of hard samples according to their frequencies, thereby mitigating dominance by infrequent but difficult-to-classify proposals. Secondly, the integration of BNPS results in consistent performance gains, along with a significant reduction in iteration sampling variability and abrupt performance shifts. Comprehensive experiments conducted on VRD datasets failed to yield notable gains using conventional techniques such as Batch Hard Negative Mining and Self-supervised Learning for proposal balancing. Consequently, we established BNPS as a pioneering solution to these VRD optimization challenges. Specifically, our results showed that BNPS led to performance improvements of up to 5.3% mAP and 3.8% mAP on VRD-100K and VRD-1M, respectively, merely through the optimization process. A thorough examination by experts in the field also led to the development of several innovative and complex architectures in the VRD domain, thereby highlighting the versatility and practicality of the proposed technique (see the supplementary document for further details). Overall, the average performance gains achieved using BNPS, across multiple datasets and various comparison methods, amounted to 3.9% mAP. By leveraging various transfer learning methods to analyze the behavior and robustness of the optimized models, we observed notable variations in accuracy among different models, thereby indicating the presence of overfitting. Consequently, the average performance losses observed upon exposure to perturbations amounted to 12.6% mAP, 10.3% mAP, and 15.3% mAP for VRD-100K, VRD-1M, and Mini-VRD, respectively. By means of a high-performance system comprising 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, we achieved a processing speed of approximately 261 frames per second on VRD-100K, thereby highlighting the practicality and versatility of the proposed technique. Implementing neural network architectures on large graphs proves computationally costly, prompting the use of distributed architectures. However, the associated communication overhead poses a significant challenge, prompting researchers to explore new approaches. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework known as Adaptive Graph Neural Networks, targeting reduction of both communication overhead and computational cost. By selectively sampling graph nodes and adapting network architecture based on non-zero gradient magnitudes, our approach eliminates unnecessary computations and node samplings, thus minimizing both communication overhead and computational cost. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our solution surpasses existing distributed GNN architectures in terms of model complexity, communication overhead, and accuracy, yielding a considerable speedup. Furthermore, our model exhibits superior generalization capabilities due to its ability to dynamically adjust the sampling ratio and adaptivity based on local and global information. As a rapidly evolving field, Quantum Deep Learning holds immense promise due to its ability to leverage both quantum and deep learning technologies. Despite this potential, there remain significant research gaps that hinder widespread adoption from the machine learning community. This survey aims to address these concerns by providing an in-depth overview of Quantum Deep Learning. The authors examined and compared various quantum deep learning models, assessed their challenges, evaluated existing repositories, benchmarks, and software frameworks, and identified future research directions. Key obstacles were found to stem from the differing environments of quantum and classical deep learning, as well as a lack of suitable datasets and testing tools. In response, the authors suggest establishing a benchmark suite and research agenda to foster collaboration and advance the field. They also propose the name 'Denotational Quantum Deep Learning' as a framework that integrates quantum and classical perspectives. The objective is to facilitate a unified approach to QDL, thereby promoting shared understanding and research harmony. Moving forward, the authors believe that open research, shared knowledge, and collaboration are essential to propelling Quantum Deep Learning forward. The authors hope this work provides a comprehensive overview, promotes research synergy, and promotes a harmonious research environment. A high-energy Muon Collider has the potential to be a leading particle physics facility in the future, however, its design faces significant challenges due to the inherent properties of muons.  A major problem is its short lifetime, requiring extremely close spacing between muon creation points and extremely high energy transfer per beam to achieve adequate energy loss, leading to intense energy release and extremely hot, dense media that must quickly cool to prevent heat damage.  A proposed initial configuration with 1.5 TeV center-of-mass energy and an luminosity of $10^{32}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ involves many complex components such as very long muon creation channels called "discovery channels," very hot, dense media called "muon cockles," and extremely powerful cooling systems called "power muon channels."  A detailed study of a possible facility design has shown that a large, multi-stage facility requiring a large amount of land and significant construction is needed to accomplish this ambitious goal.  A large, full-scale mock-up of the initial configuration called the "PRISM muon," which features a large, long facility called "PRISM," has been constructed and is now on display at Fermilab to help learn and understand the design requirements of a high-energy Muon Collider through hands-on observation and education.  A series of muon-related educational programs and public events are being planned at the PRISM muon to promote learning and understanding the design requirements of a high-energy Muon Collider through on-site observation and education. This study updates previous work by calling for a re-evaluation of existing experiments in the context of dark matter research, primarily focusing on the conditions under which the low-energy tail might be distinguishable from background noise within upcoming X-ray experiments. Specifically, we analyzed the potential detection of this Hawking radiation by the AXPC, CTD, and eROSITA experiments, finding that significant integration times would be required to identify the signal. As a result, we conclude that the search for this Hawking radiation represents a test of the theories of quantum gravity and primordial black holes, though it may not be within reach of current or upcoming X-ray experiments to verify the predictions of Hawking radiation for dark matter research. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the signal might be identifiable in the spectra of individual stars, though this would depend on detectable levels of radiation from primordial black holes within a given stellar system. sequential model than previously thought. We attributed this discrepancy to the
processor's overhead in handling simple operations and the need to perform extra
operations in the pipeline model. We proposed a new model, requiring a pipelined
processor to start a new instruction only when the previous one has been completed,

We demonstrate a PTAS for optimizing general-valued CSPs with crisp constraints, meeting the criteria established by Kolmogorov and Riemann (FOCS 2013) and Riemann (STOC 2014). Furthermore, our findings also yield a PTAS for minimizing and maximizing summation-valued CSPs with arbitrary small target values, along with approximation algorithms for certain subproblems, leading to improved approximation ratios for specific constraint types such as sums of primes or powers. The work is further expanded to include a PTAS for a more comprehensive class of general-valued CSPs with certain types of arbitrary (non-crisp) constraints. All mentioned algorithms are shown to have a relative gap of O(log^k K) for k-ary constraints, where K represents the size of the solution. Finally, we present an approximation algorithm for a general-valued CSP with arbitrary (non-crisp) constraints, achieving an approximation ratio of O(log^k K) for k-ary constraints. These results are derived using an iterative framework involving modular optimization problems, the PTAS for which is based on an approach combining flagship algorithms and the epsilon-nested disjunctions structure introduced by Riemann et al. An alternative, more efficient algorithm is developed, leading to a more streamlined and efficient PTAS, thereby illustrating a more practical approach to solving modular optimization problems in the context of general-valued CSPs. Verifiable, open-ended problem statements are provided, focusing on potential improvements to our approximation ratios and the development of better algorithms for minimizing general-valued CSPs. These problem statements serve as a basis for proposed future research directions. In an effort to decrease the need for extensive annotation in computer vision tasks, particularly parsing, we introduce FPIO. FPIO is a novel few-shot parsing model that leverages a practical machine-learning approach known as structure-encoded learning. It achieves this by incorporating a simplified structure encoder and integrating metric learning into a conventional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). This innovative design empowers FPIO to derive parsing outcomes solely based on visual features derived from a generic object classifier, eliminating the need for extra layers or input image resizing commonly seen in other approaches. FPIO outperforms existing few-shot parsing techniques while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, it demonstrates superior generalization capabilities on parsing tasks involving objects not seen during training, showcasing its effectiveness in a variety of real-world applications with a minimal amount of annotated data. Specifically, it achieves top results on the few-shot parsing benchmark, yielding a 2.9% and 2.6% relative improvement over the rival FSPar and CoSE methods, respectively, when trained using just 50 annotated image masks. Even when supplied with 100 annotated masks, it still outperforms FSPar by 1.2%, further highlighting its efficacy. Semantic segmentation tasks in real-world scenarios benefit significantly from the detailed information provided by hyperspectral images. Their various bands can serve several purposes: enhance distinct objects, reduce ambiguity in areas with mixed features, or indicate specific object attributes. Nevertheless, current deep learning-based approaches typically disregard the object attributes embedded in the images. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel hyperspectral semantic segmentation task that employs refined labels to target specific attributes. We demonstrate the feasibility of this task by developing a new hyperspectral semantic segmentation model, HSS-Net, which utilizes object attributes to guide the segmentation process. Through extensive experiments on three datasets, we show that our proposed model surpasses the performance of other state-of-the-art models. The improved performance is attributed to the detailed information provided by hyperspectral images, which facilitates more accurate object attribute labeling, in turn enhancing the segmentation results. To facilitate replication of our findings, we provide our model implementation and the three dataset files used in the study. Additionally, an online hyperspectral semantic segmentation demo is available for use. The detailed information can be accessed at: https://github.com/IndigoTeam/HSS-Net. The coronal activity of KIC 9267654, an G-type star with a distinct rotation pattern, is examined via analysis of X-ray light curves obtained from the ROSAT satellite. This analysis yields evidence of prolonged outbursts lasting between 140 and 170 days that are present in all relevant light curves. Interestingly, these coronal activity fluctuations coincide with changes in the star's shadow transits as observed by the Kepler space telescope, with their respective periods aligning with the star's unique rotation pattern. Although the 130-day cycle of coronal activity does not clearly match any known astronomical periods, its duration is suggestive of a star shadow or tidal interaction influenced by a companion planet, as seen in stars like KIC 1120577861 and Kepler-1167. We conclude to keep interpreting the observed phenomena as a result of pulsation-related activities, although the possibility of a stellar activity cycle or other novel phenomena also exists. We strongly advise further investigation into this novel celestial phenomenon through observations, data analysis, and computational simulations. The observed data and light curves are available to download on the CASA website (casa.uva.es). Additionally, the ROSAT data are accessible through the HEASARC website (heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov). This research focuses on a Random Access Machine model that can process polynomial integers, in addition to natural numbers, within a single memory location. We demonstrate that this model, incorporating modular arithmetic, can solve the Problem of Computing Greatest Common Divisors (GCD) in linear time, specifically O(n), when using a fixed modulus value. This outcome builds on a prior discovery showing that the same model could perform modular arithmetic operations in linear time. Moreover, we successfully devise a novel algorithm to compute the product of all integers within a given range, both for both fixed and variable moduli cases, in linear time as well. This finding benefits from the capability to efficiently sample random integers within that range in constant time. As an additional application, we devise an algorithm to determine if a given integer within a specific range is prime, accomplishing this task in linear time when the range is very large in comparison to the moduli value. This innovative algorithm draws inspiration from the AKS primality test, incorporating key elements such as the probability of incorrectly classifying a composite number as prime, along with specific bounds on the number of required computations. Lastly, we successfully adapt this probabilistic primality test to be deterministic, achieving the same linear time efficiency by exploring all possible moduli values systematically. As an added benefit, we also present a new, deterministic algorithm for testing primality of a single integer, leveraging the capabilities of the model to perform polynomial integer arithmetic efficiently. This novel approach, inspired by the AKS primality test, requires exponentially fewer computations overall. However, the number of required operations still grows linearly with the size of the input integer. Furthermore, we successfully devise an algorithm to compute the greatest common divisor of two polynomial integers, achieving a linear time efficiency when the degree of one integer is significantly lower than the degree of the other. Lastly, we explore the connections between the computational complexity of the model using modular arithmetic and the fundamental theoretical concepts of fields, extending this understanding to the model's capability of handling polynomial integers, before concluding with future directions and potential applications. Session-based recommendation systems are particularly challenging due to the absence of global user data, making it crucial to leverage user-specific information from limited historical interactions within short-term sessions.  Current methods in session-based recommendation focus primarily on utility-driven session optimization, with little regard for broader data augmentation through self-supervision that could aid in representative session generation.  To address this gap, our work introduces an innovative self-supervised framework that leverages an additional auxiliary task to analyze optimized session content.  By leveraging multiple self-supervised criteria across distinct temporal dimensions within optimized sessions, our model is capable of generating representative, expanded datasets that improve recommendation system performance, as corroborated by our experimental findings across multiple real-world benchmarks.  Notably, our model is transferable and exhibits compatible or enhanced performance when used as a standalone recommendation model. We also determine the parameters of these LCD codes, given which group G and constancy $\lambda$ are employed. Additionally, we analyze the rates of these constancy-based LCD codes and find that they approach 1 when $\lambda$ approaches 0. We further investigate the existence of linear compression modules in group rings, facilitating the construction of group ring-based LCD codes, for which we provide rate and complexity bounds. This article outlines a detailed calculation of the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, $GL_{\infty}$, using the properties of invariant differential forms from the action of $S_{\infty}$ on an auxiliary complex. We have adopted the perspective of Borel's cohomology for the action of $S_{\infty}$ on $C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{\infty})$, where $C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{\infty})$ serves as the space of all continuous functions from the permutation group $\mathbb{R}^{\infty}$ to itself that are based on an arbitrary finite set of elements. We have identified pure and mixed Symm-GROUP invariants, where Symm denotes the symplectic group, and these forms' properties will serve as the foundation for future research on the real cohomology of various geometric and Lie groups. Additionally, the article confirms the Markowitz theorem through Borel's cohomology and offers an innovative approach to understanding the theorem's contribution to the stable real cohomology of $GL_{\infty}$. As a direct result of our findings, we have generalised the theorem to all Lie groups representing simple rational homotopy types. We have also determined the stable real cohomology of all general linear groups, where the findings extend beyond the realm of Lie theory, offering novel insights into the Symm-GROUP invariants' structure. Specifically, our research has allowed us to formulate hypotheses regarding the Symm-GROUP invariants' structure when acting on $C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{\infty})$ and provided an accurate prediction of their multiplication properties. By combining these insights with the properties of the Symm-GROUP invariants, we have successfully calculated the real cohomology of the semigroup of upper triangular matrices. Our article concludes with a discussion of the prospective applications of our study to the fields of topological homotopy theory and geometric topology. We have provided formal connections between our primary findings and various notable theories in these fields. Some of these connections are confirmed while others are merely conjectural. Researchers have questioned the efficacy of auxiliary variables in training recurrent neural networks, arguing that they often serve as an unintended workaround for issues with vanishing gradients and limited context for object categorization tasks. This study seeks to provide an explanation for their significance through theoretical analysis and a range of empirical evaluations. By introducing a bi-directional context attention model, we successfully eliminated the need for auxiliary variables in recurrent neural networks, achieving comparable performance without their use. Notably, this innovation improved the performance of deep recurrent networks on standard benchmarks, surpassing existing state-of-the-art results on ImageNet for the first time. Moreover, our proposed model yielded impressive results on other benchmarks, encompassing multi-label and vehicle classification, outperforming competing methods that employed auxiliary variables. By analyzing the effects of varying model parameters on performance, we observed a direct correlation between the obtained accuracy and increased context coverage for object categorization. Consequently, our proposed model has become the new benchmark for deep recurrent neural networks, providing an open-source implementation at the specified URL. Moreover, our study highlights the critical role of auxiliary variables in enabling deep recurrent networks to leverage their expanded memory capacity for object categorization, empowering a range of deep recurrent neural networks to achieve state-of-the-art performance with the aid of these variables. Finally, our proposed model has a range of practical applications, including enabling deep recurrent networks to achieve high accuracy on vehicle classification in real-world scenarios and surpassing existing state-of-the-art results on multi-label object classification benchmarks. Additional details regarding the implementation and evaluation of our proposed model can be found in the associated technical report at the specified URL. Based on our empirical findings, successfully integrating bi-directional context attention models into recurrent neural networks appears to be the most effective approach to eliminating the need for auxiliary variables in object categorization tasks without sacrificing performance. Therefore, we anticipate our proposed model to serve as a starting point for future research in this domain, providing a range of open-source implementations at the specified URL that researchers can freely utilize and adapt for their own studies. In particular, our proposed model has potential applications in vehicle reidentification, object classification, image recognition, vehicle identification, and material recognition, among other domains where visual data is utilized. Additionally, our study may be of interest to researchers working on image segmentation using recurrent neural networks, as well as researchers focused on object detection, who may leverage our proposed model to achieve state-of-the-art performance with the aid of bi-directional context attention models. In the investigation, Higgs boson signal strengths towards these vector particles are compared against the standard model predictions, with constraints obtained through the ratio of observed to expected cross-sections, resulting in observed significances ranging from 1.04 to 1.47 standard deviations across the various investigations. Consequently, the Higgs boson couplings to vector bosons were found to be within the following ranges: HW = 0.75^+0.28-0.27, HZ = 0.99^+0.24-0.20, and Hgamma = 0.53^+0.29-0.20 in the most constrained scenario, with standard model expectations ranging from 0.78 to 0.87. Furthermore, the study evaluated Higgs boson couplings to vector bosons in favour of the standard model expectations, with possible suppression of these couplings relative to the standard model expectations when considering the most constrained scenario. Additionally, the study evaluated possible suppression of these couplings relative to the standard model expectations for specific CP-odd trilinear Higgs boson couplings. Identifying differences between images without knowing where they differ is a task called unsupervised change detection. Using only pairs of images and a mask to exclude changes is not efficient in real-world scenarios where multiple images are involved. On the other hand, supervised methods offer great results but need constant updates as new classes are discovered. We compare the effectiveness of unsupervised change detection to supervised methods, revealing similar outcomes with unsupervised methods performing well on individual map layers, especially when spectral values are analyzed. Notably, great results can be achieved without any prior knowledge of the area, making unsupervised change detection a viable option. Consider integers $a$ and $b$, with $0 \leq a < b$, and let $n$ be a positive integer. We aim to count how many ways there are to express $n$ as a sum of a square and an additive complement of $b$. This problem is equivalent to finding representations of integers of the form $n+ab^2$ as sums of two squares. We investigate the asymptotic distribution of these representations and provide an asymptotic formula that holds for all $n$ and a significant portion of integers $a$ and $b$. This formula refines a previous finding by Chen, Kong, and Sissons, whose work was supported in part by the Laura Nash Foundation. Additionally, we offer a standalone asymptotic formula that counts the number of ways to express $n$ as a sum of a square and an additive complement of $b$. This formula is comparable in form to Pearson's asymptotic formula for counting representations of integers as sums of two squares. To derive these results, we leveraged an innovative strategy introduced by Chen et al., involving the averaging of exponential sums, as well as distinct measures of weight $1/2$. We also established an novel connection between certain binary sequences and the counting problem at hand, which was made possible by the computation of certain sumsets within the sequence. Our proof also requires the evaluation of certain lattices, which in turn necessitates an analysis of certain minimal code words within those lattices. Furthermore, our work led to the derivation of several complementary results, including a criterion that isolates a substantial class of $a$ and $b$ values for which our asymptotic formula holds, as well as a general asymptotic formula that holds for a broad class of congrence classes for $a$ and $b$. Our analysis also yields the derivation of several additional lattices, which in turn enable the counting of a certain class of representations of integers as sums of squares and additive complements of $b$. We investigate similar problems in our ongoing research. Currently, we are studying a generalization of the problem in which an integer $c$ is also incorporated, effectively examining representations of integers of the form $n+abc^2$ as sums of two squares. Our research on this topic is ongoing and may yield new and interesting results. Our study of this generalized problem could provide valuable insights into both discrete algebraic geometry and the geometry of codes. By placing group IVI elements in the center of a silicon crystal lattice, researchers gain insight into how spin exchange interacts through neighboring bonds.  The central role played by the light elements in the exchange interaction is highlighted, and a quantitative relationship between the central element's atomic number and the strength of the exchange interaction is identified.  The magnitude of the exchange interaction depends on the central element, and the overall pattern suggests that the Heisenberg interaction's direction remains consistent.  The data collected through advanced numerical techniques, such as the variational Monte Carlo method and the exact diagonalization method, reveals that the characteristics of the Heisenberg interaction's ground state remain consistent at various temperatures.  The central element's placement significantly affects the exchange interaction's anisotropy, but the Heisenberg interaction's characteristics remain isotropic in nature.  The experimental detection of this anisotropic exchange interaction may be feasible using NMR techniques.  The research made possible by the theoretical simulation of the silicon crystal lattice's dopants provides valuable insight into how the place of the dopants affects the Heisenberg interaction's anisotropy.  The study of the group IVI-doped silicon crystal lattices could serve as a model for understanding the principles of the anisotropic exchange interaction.  The potential of incorporating the anisotropic exchange interaction into quantum computation schemes, particularly to create points of high curvature in a spin droplet, is explored.  The incorporation of the anisotropic exchange interaction could significantly decrease the droplet's coherence lifetime, but the efficient manipulation of the droplet may also be improved through its association with a mobile spin.  The potential of utilizing the anisotropic exchange interaction to create small, movable qubits could be key in developing droplet-based quantum computing systems. This paper presents the open-source library LibOPT for benchmarking sequence optimization algorithms, offering a diverse set of optimization tasks along with comprehensive comparison tools. Currently, the library boasts a range of benchmarking functions, including 28 optimization problems across various domains such as protein structure prediction, protein design, molecular structure optimization, graph optimization, and combinatorial optimization. Additionally, LibOPT provides a pluggable architecture that enables the incorporation of various optimization algorithms and objective functions, enabling researchers to systematically evaluate the performance of their algorithms on a variety of benchmarks. By utilizing LibOPT, we conducted an empirical study to identify potential issues with the existing benchmarks and noted notable differences in performance across multiple benchmarks, highlighting the potential of the library for advancing research in sequence optimization and facilitating fair comparisons between different algorithms. The source code of LibOPT is freely accessible on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT License. Currently, the library supports optimization algorithms written in Python but is designed to be easily adaptable to other programming languages. Future updates to LibOPT will incorporate user feedback to ensure continuous improvement and expansion of the library's capabilities. Additionally, the repository includes a tutorial, detailed documentation, and a set of guided exercises for beginners to quickly understand the functionality and effectiveness of LibOPT in solving real-world sequence optimization problems.
