This article provides an update on the transitivity degree for specific types of varieties, specifically for cubic surfaces, del Pezzo surfaces of higher degrees, and hypersurfaces in small numbers of variables. The proof method involves using a structure theorem that was previously defined. From this, it's possible to derive and calculate the maximum number of transitive actions for each of these varieties using a method called 'back computation.' Additionally, the article determines the highest possible value of the transitivity degree for del Pezzo surfaces of degree 8 in three variables and for cubic surfaces in four variables. It's also shown that there are no transitive actions on surfaces that are nonsingular and of degree 7 in four variables, or on surfaces that are nonsingular and of degree 8 in three variables. For varieties that are not smooth, such as cubic surfaces with a single ordinary double singularity, the article determines the transitivity degree precisely and finds it to be 21, and it's conjectured that this figure will remain the maximum for non-smooth del Pezzo surfaces of degree 8. These mathematical findings are expressed in an abstract and supported by accompanying theorems. Finally, the article concludes by addressing hypersurfaces of degree 10 in three variables and finding the transitivity degree for these to be 46. Also, it's noted that there are no transitive actions on surfaces that are nonsingular and of degree 9 in three variables. This leads to the hypothesis that the figures calculated represent the maximum possible transitive actions for these specific types of algebraic surfaces. These mathematical findings possess potential and may be developed further into valuable contributions to the field of algebraic geometry. It's also proposed that this method could be extended for use in studying other types of algebraic varieties. To this end, a new field of research is introduced, focused on the study of varieties that admit a transitive action, denoted as Set-Theoretic Complete intersections (STCIs). An example is presented of a variety, specifically a surface that is not smooth, which has a set-theoretic complete intersection property but does not possess the property of being smooth. These varieties provide a useful framework within which to study the relationship between degree and action types. This concept opens the door for potential and interesting research in the field of algebraic geometry. Last but not least, a new area for study is introduced, focused on the classification and study of varieties that admit a transitive action. Unlike abelian situations, where total momentum is clearly defined as the sum of individual momenta, in non-abelian cases, a clear definition of total momentum is lacking. However, recent research revealed that in all cases, including those with gauge symmetry, a total momentum is defined as a quadratic expression of individual particle momenta. We're exploring a novel approach to derive this total momentum operator without resorting to ad-hoc methods. Instead, we're defining a total momentum operator as a canonical commutator of a Hamiltonian operator, which we'll demonstrate applies to both particle and antiparticle systems in any spin system, any potential scenario, and any number of particles. We'll also show how this total momentum operator enables accurate calculation of its square, which wasn't previously possible. As a significant consequence, our research will facilitate the accurate calculation of scattering cross-talks in non-abelian theories, a practical application of our findings. We establish the solvability of the BSDE with a generator influenced by past values, which encompasses both backward stochastic differential equations and certain types of recursive type stochastic differential equations. Our solution allows for a degree of state-space dimension increase. Additionally, it's demonstrated that the inclusion of prior values in the BSDE's generator corresponds to a form of memory in the equation. Our analysis of BSDEs with memory may be seen as an extension of the study on backward stochastic evolution equations, which itself builds upon the fundamental work of Bismut-Atares in the context of infinite-dimensional backward stochastic differential equations. Our method of proof involves introducing an approximation technique, which is an adaptation of the one used by Pardoux-Touzi for infinite-dimensional BSDEs. This technique itself relies on the combination of several key tools, including a version of the Kawazuke-Shinai theorem, and an approach for dealing with degenerate elliptic equations in infinite-dimensional spaces that draws inspiration from the work of Da Prato-Zambotti-Zaucer. Our work also extends the research on forward stochastic differential equations with a generator influenced by past values, which is an extension of the study on forward stochastic differential equations by the same authors. Our approach to dealing with this type of equation involves using a similar approximation technique as for the BSDE to prove comparison and convergence theorems. These theorems are analogous to those for forward stochastic differential equations, but are adapted for the context of equations influenced by past values. This type of equation may be seen as an extension of the backward Ward-Stokey model, which is commonly used in the field of economics to deal with infinite horizon consumption investment problems that are subject to certain constraints such as a kink constraint. In order to responsibly ensure that autonomous systems function correctly in various scenarios, it is essential to evaluate their robustness. This study utilizes dynamics models trained on real-world data from a robotic arm moving in a 2D environment to test its robustness by introducing virtual manipulations. By incorporating a likelihood constraint on the model's predictive ability, the research finds that a minimum threshold for this constraint significantly improves the arm's resistance to physical disruptions, particularly when interacting with objects in the environment. Additionally, controlling the contact force during these interactions also shows promising results, highlighting the potential for model-based control to increase both safety and robustness. This study's findings have implications for the practical application of learned dynamics models in autonomous systems, suggesting that these models can support responsible decision-making from both a legal and ethical standpoint. Ultimately, the research presents a novel evaluation metric that balances performance and robustness, demonstrating its practicality through empirical validation. This work was partially presented at the 2020 IEEE/RSJ Annual Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems. Additional findings were submitted for review at the 2021 International Conference on Robotics and Automation. Both sets of findings are integrated into this thesis. Additional context is provided in Chapters 7 and 8, with relevant code and data available online for reproduction. Most importantly, this research seeks to promote the development of autonomous systems that are both safe and robust. By examining the interplay between virtual manipulations and real-world interactions, this thesis showcases the potential for model-based control to increase the practicality of learned dynamics models in practical applications. In doing so, this research seeks to promote the responsible development of autonomous systems capable of addressing complex challenges over the long term, as detailed in Chapter 9. In keeping with this goal, the primary contribution of this research consists of multiple, interconnected findings rather than a singular one, as presented in successive chapters. A new approach involves applying descriptive combinatorial methods to analyze and categorize efficient coded caching schemes. Within a general framework, centralizing extensive combinatorial data allows for the exploration of potentially optimal caching schemes. By focusing on the subcombining schemes, which are cached content combinations determined by the scheme, various extremal problems can be identified. These problems can then be used to pinpoint the most efficient caching schemes. By applying similar principles to the most basic of combinatorial objects, specific parameters related to coded caching can be derived. These principles offer a versatile method for studying coded caching schemes, allowing for the identification of specific cases and subcases within the larger combinatorial landscape. Ultimately, this analysis provides a thorough understanding of the optimal caching schemes, and their characteristics in relation to the fundamental parameters of coded caching. Additionally, this framework can be adapted for studying placement driving caching schemes, which prioritize maintaining user information over shared content. By exploring the potential of combinatorial analysis, new placement driving caching schemes have been developed, and their corresponding parameters derived. These schemes represent an area for further research and development in the coded caching field. Ultimately, this framework and its findings can be used for implementing caching systems in real-world applications. Two such applications, where the proposed framework can be implemented, are network security and online advertising. Network security involves combating malware spread on network nodes, and online advertising involves targeting online users. By applying the framework to these problems, new placement driving caching schemes have been developed for both issues. Specifically, for network security, an integrated combinatorial approach involving epidemiology was used to develop a caching scheme. For online advertising, a combination of combinatorial analysis and target identification was employed to develop a caching system. These applications represent just two of the numerous domains where the proposed framework can be implemented to develop new coded caching schemes. Currently, research is underway to develop a tool to aid in the implementation of the framework within real-world contexts. The framework itself, along with the scheme parameters and scheme combinations, can be found at the website, coded cachings dot com. Additionally, open source code for the tool is located at the website, github dot com, under the username 'coded-cachings'. Three specific applications where the proposed framework can be implemented are multimedia streaming, online advertising, and network security. By applying the framework to these problems, new placement driving caching schemes have been developed, specifically for multimedia and network security. These schemes represent just a few of the numerous areas for further research and development in the coded caching field

The Scott model has provided a fundamental construction for studying types and meanings within a predicative and constructive framework. Past research utilized the Scott model to investigate programming languages and categories, yet it lacked an explicit connection to programming languages themselves. More recent work by Ahier and co-authors established a method for defining types and meanings as domains within a constructive type theory. In this current research, we build upon their study by showing that the Scott model can be represented within a constructive type theory, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of programming languages as part of a larger predicative framework. We demonstrate the utility of this representation by outlining a method for translating predicative and constructive types to types expressed in the Coq proof assistant. Additionally, we explore an alternative representation of the Scott model as a collection of families of domains, adhering to a strong normalisation condition, and examine its potential as a framework for automatic type inference. In contrast to prior attempts using type higher inclusions, this family structure offers a more natural framework for understanding the concept of type inference. We claim that the Scott model, when combined with the principles of predicativity and constructivity, provides a more robust and natural foundation for type theory than previous attempts at developing type-inferable type theories. We also briefly discuss and motivate the integration of a small amount of additional structure, drawn from higher-order logic, as required for understanding the concept of extensional equality within a predicative framework. We outline a method for defining extensional equality as a collection of families of domain-valued families, as opposed to a family of domains-valued families, as initially proposed by Seely, and show that this alternative structure is equivalent to the original. We represent this new structure within a constructive type theory and prove that it is consistent with the principles of predicativity and constructivity. We also establish a method for translating this representation to the Coq proof assistant. This paper presents a novel framework for creating a universal collision avoidance filter that can be applied to a variety of robotics tasks. Our method incorporates the spatial geometry of mobile robotic arms, enabling precise trajectory modeling and efficient collision avoidance strategies. The framework models the robotic arm as a simplified geometric structure, using a universal function to generate trajectories that adapt to varying arm lengths and configurations. This allows our filter to function seamlessly with common motion planning algorithms, such as PRISM, demonstrating a significant reduction in execution time and improved resilience to collisions in challenging environments, especially with under-actuated arms. Our approach achieves a notable speed improvement of up to 66% and reduces the risk of collisions by 75% when compared to existing collision avoidance methods. Additionally, our geometric-based approach offers improved flexibility and adaptability over existing, task-specific filters. general overview of cybernetics, its current state, and the research focus at the
Novosibirsk Academic Research Institute of Cybernetics. The recent breakthrough
involved developing a novel cybernetic solution for natural language processing
invariance, addressing the challenges posed by significant linguistic and contextual
diversity across various written and spoken forms. The developed theory and
experimental results substantiate the feasibility of this innovation. Additionally,
the researchers explored the potential for controlling small systems composed of
neural cells, utilizing a cybernetic approach. They identified a promising model for
its implementation and are currently working on achieving control over a small
cell ensemble. Furthermore, the institute's research focus encompasses extensive
analyses of the brain's functional and structural dynamics across various scales,
from individual cells to systemic interactions, all essential for understanding the
complex human mind. These topics are currently being studied using advanced
computational methods, coupled with advanced medical imaging and clinical data. 
Lastly, the report highlights the institute's research focus on cybernetic solutions
for managing and coordinating large projects, its experience in providing expertize
to various industries, and the newly introduced educational programs in cybernetics. 
These initiatives are pivotal for fostering innovative environments and making the
most of available scientific potential. The presentation concluded with an open-door
policy, inviting the audience to participate in the institute's research and
collaborative efforts.

Hadamard gates, used in Ramsey interferometry with Bose-Einstein condensates, can be implemented in various ways, such as through optical tweezers or spin-dependent potentials, by utilizing time-varying patterns. In the context of spin-dependent potentials, the nonlinearity of the interaction between the condensate's atomic spin components results in an enhanced performance in Ramsey interferometry beyond the traditional coherent states' capabilities. This improvement is attributed to multi-atomic spin entanglements formed over time, leading to a greater destructive interference and, consequently, a sharper minimum in interference patterns. This unique property of nonlinear systems may hold potential for applications in quantum metrology utilizing complex many-body states. After discussing the basic concepts of Ramsey interferometry with BECs, we delve into the optical implementation of a nonlinear Hadamard gate using a standing wave pattern in a cavity, and explore its limitations imposed by cavity losses and atomic relaxations. The study provides a roadmap for the realization of coherent many-body states via optical interactions, contributing to the fields of quantum computing and quantum metrology. Moreover, the research paves the way for the exploration of other intriguing phenomena in cold atomic systems, such as nonlinear state transformations, entanglements, and interactions. Lastly, the work is especially relevant due to the burgeoning field of optomechanics in mesoscopic systems, as it has the potential to extend its principles to systems with mechanical degrees of freedom. In this work, we explore an approach that adapts Gröbner basis algorithms to compute solutions to a polynomial system by utilizing signature-based methods, such as Buchberger's algorithm and GBASIC, and incorporating flags that track crucial characteristics throughout the computation process. We then examine two main strategies for applying these flags in order to efficiently terminate the calculation when desired, as well as propose two methods for effectively extracting the full information needed to solve the polynomial system even after the termination flags have been activated. We further determine the complexity of each strategy and assess their practical effectiveness through computational tests. We show that one of the strategies allows for an efficient and straightforward implementation that takes only O(N log N) time, where N represents the total degree of the polynomials in the system. We further refine this result to show that in specific scenarios where certain conditions are met, the time complexity can be reduced to O(N). We demonstrate that our approach outperforms other methods through various computational examples. We further provide a description of how this technique can be applied in the context of Gröbner bases for ideals containing a parametric element, effectively reducing the leading degree variable in many instances, thus potentially simplifying the computation. We showcase the application of this method to solve two complex problems, one of which originates from the field of Statistics and the other from the study of algebraic surfaces. Our work thus offers an innovative and time-saving solution that can effectively employ signature-based Gröbner basis algorithms to compute polynomial system solutions. We thereby revive and enhance a previously proposed method. Our approach also offers an alternative perspective to the state-of-the-art algorithm, SRES, and successfully resolves the identified complexity issue associated with this method. Our results thus offer insights into the Gröbner basis algorithm, SRES, and provide an application example to the study of algebraic surfaces, in addition to providing an innovative solution to previously complex problems in the field of algebraic geometry. Our approach is implemented in the computer algebra software, MAGMA, under the name Gröbner Basis Flags. We thereby provide an essential tool that facilitates the computation of solutions to polynomial systems through various algorithms. Our software thus offers an invaluable resource that complements the existing algorithm, SRES, in addition to offering new strategies for terminating the calculation and extracting solution information, thus offering further possibilities for algorithmic interactions. The number of photons produced in Cu+Cu collisions at 200 GeV has been compared to charged particle production in Au+Au collisions at the same energy level. Inclusive spectra of photons, separated into prompt and non-prompt components, are presented in various rapidity and transverse momentum ranges. The rapidity density of photons, ignoring the contribution from the fireball, increased more steeply with participant number than charged particle production, and, at the same energy level, non-prompt photon spectra fell more rapidly with increasing rapidity than those observed in Au+Au collisions. In Cu+Cu collisions, the ratio of the non-prompt component to the total photon spectrum was significantly lower than in Au+Au collisions, and, on average, accounted for approximately 30% of the total, as opposed to 50% in Au+Au collisions. The measured spectra are consistent with the prediction that an increasing number of particles per nucleon participates in the collision, and suggest a significant contribution from the fireball in Cu+Cu. Additionally, the observed phenomena may be linked to the phase transition between quark and hadronic matter in medium-sized collisions. Finally, the measured spectra are more suggestive of a collective phenomenon in photon production rather than a purely geometric effect. Photon spectra, combined with measurements of jet quenching and elliptical flow in Cu+Cu collisions, offer compelling evidence for an interaction between high transverse momentum particles and the created medium, and raise the prospect of detecting a similar effect in Pb+Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.52 GeV. Furthermore, the measurement of non-prompt photon spectra in Pb+Pb collisions at the LHC energies may provide further insight into the interaction between high transverse momentum particles and the created medium. Finally, the presented data are compared to data collected in p+Pb collisions at the LHC, and to calculations incorporating various physical processes in p+Pb and Pb+Pb collisions. This paper delves into extremal properties of certain hypergraph configurations. Specifically, it investigates the maximum possible number of edges in a hypergraph that avoids specific subgraphs, and also explores the maximum possible number of edges in a hypergraph that contains certain specified subgraphs. These investigations are conducted within the context of K_4^3-free hypergraphs, which are hypergraphs that do not feature certain prohibited subgraphs known as K_4^3. Initially, it is established that exco_2(n,H) = exco_2(n,K_4^3), where exco_2(n,H) represents the maximum possible number of edges in a hypergraph of a given type (in this case, K_4^3-free or matching H) over all such hypergraphs. A key component of the study involves determining an exact value for exco_2(n,K_4^3). It is further discovered that this problem is equivalent to a previously investigated concept, pilo_2(n), which itself is an unsolved problem. A near optimal value for exco_2(n,K_4^3) is eventually determined through an intricate analysis of hypergraph configurations consisting of small subgraphs. Additionally, a method for systematically determining exact values for exco_2(n,H) in cases where the associated hypergraph configuration, H, is comprised of small subgraphs is presented. This approach is itself an iterative solution to a previously associated problem, exco_1(n,H), which itself is an unsolved problem. A near optimal value for exco_1(n,K_4^3) is also presented as a result of this study. More generally, it is established that exco_1(n,H) can be determined precisely for any hypergraph configuration, H, consisting of edges containing fewer than n^{\frac{1}{5}+\varepsilon} vertices, where \varepsilon > 0. This is accomplished through an examination of the maximum possible number of edges in a hypergraph of a given type (in this case, M_{k,\bar{\delta}}^n, where \bar{\delta} is a fixed constant) over all such hypergraphs. A key component of the study involves determining an exact value for exco_1(M_{k,\bar{\delta}}^n). Finally, a near optimal value for exco_1(n,K_4^3) is presented as a result of this study. This research introduces an advanced algorithm for drawing line segments with precise, uniformly wide fan-shaped joins. Unlike existing methods that can result in misaligned fan shapes, this new algorithm ensures a smooth, uniform width for the joins by employing a series of connected arcs. We have analyzed the computational complexity of this algorithm and found it to be O(n log n), with the ability to be optimized to O(n) through the use of a sweep line approach. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of the new algorithm with existing methods for drawing line segments, demonstrating that our approach offers significantly improved visual clarity and reducing drawing time by up to 20 times. Furthermore, we have successfully implemented this new algorithm in the Matplotlib plotting library, showcasing its effectiveness through a variety of illustrative examples. A novel interpolation formula based on the radial basis function (RBF) will be introduced, differing from prior approaches. It employs an absolute value and a parameterized RBF, $r_\alpha(r,w)$, to create a continuous, smooth interpolation surface. Furthermore, this new interpolation method maintains the convexity and monotonicity of the interpolated function. Additionally, it will be demonstrated that its derivative is a piecewise linear function. A quasi-interpolation formula will also be developed from this framework, possessing the same properties. Unlike other convex RBF-based interpolation methods, the novel formulation does not involve the distance to a fixed point in space. Instead, it relies on the distance to the support domain's boundary. Consequently, it can accurately interpolate functions defined on bounded domains. Several two- and three-dimensional numerical examples will be presented to illustrate the method's effectiveness. These examples involve functions with (anti-)convex properties and demonstrate the method's superiority over existing RBF-based interpolation methods. Moreover, comparisons with the standard RBF interpolation method, as well as interpolation methods based on positive definite decomposition and a localized RBF-based interpolation method, will be presented. These experiments highlight the method's efficiency and accuracy in both low- and high-resolution scenarios. Generally, the novel interpolation method exhibited the best results, followed closely by positive definite decomposition. Finally, the implementation of the method will be discussed, including the utilization of standardized libraries for high-performance computing and engineering applications. Standardized software code is available for download at https://github.com/lalevesm/ConvexInterpolation. Several additional visualizations and examples can also be found on that repository. Specifically, additional numerical experiments are available as follows: - A three-dimensional case studying the effect of parameter $\alpha$ on the convexity of interpolated function $f_{3D}$. - A study on the quasi-interpolation method's approximation order as a function of the parameter $\alpha$. - A set of standardized tests for the software code, as recommended by the OpenTURNS project. Lastly, some preliminary findings on the potential connection between the method and the finite element method will be presented. This is evidenced by the finite difference approximation of the Laplacian operator and the potential application of the method in computing a finite element solution in two dimensions that is (semi)-convex. Further investigation into this connection is recommended. Recent studies have examined how data augmentation through mask application affects Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Researchers have concentrated on analyzing the connections between mask size, network architecture, and performance. In this study, we delved into how mask creation methods influence CNN performance, specifically exploring two methods: delimiting masks for image classification and super pixel masks for semantic segmentation. We discovered that applying masks to mid-layer features produces the most significant performance enhancements for image classification and super pixel masks for semantic segmentation, a finding not previously reported in the literature. We also identified that using mask sizes equivalent to 1/5 to 1/3 of the input image dimension yields the best results, a finding in contrast to other studies. Notably, while pre-training on augmented data improves classification performance, this improvement diminishes in subsequent training stages. We provide insights into the mask's representative power, analyze various mask creation methods, and suggest that using a fixed, optimal mask size is more effective than dynamically adjusting it based on input image dimensions. We also found that applying masks to mid-layer features produces the most significant performance enhancements for image classification and super pixel masks for semantic segmentation, a key conclusion. We hope this knowledge serves as a foundation for future research on data augmentation through mask application. The characteristic flexibility of soft robotics is simultaneously its primary benefit and limitation, as improved control could lead to greater productivity and a broader range of applications. The intricate nature of soft robots makes it difficult to model and analyze their motion dynamics, posing a significant challenge in the field. The application of the Koopman operator theory has shown promising results in this area by facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics through the use of observed states. Our research focuses on the development of a novel control method for soft robots based on the Koopman operator theory, which significantly outperforms existing boundary control methods in nonlinear systems while requiring fewer actuated modules, thus reducing energy consumption and prolonging the lifespan of the robot. The proposed control method exhibits superior spatio-temporal consistency, as evidenced by the many trials of raising a soft beam, which closely follows the desired trajectory. The presented work has potential implications for the fields of soft robotics, control systems, and boundary control, as it enables the precise control of complex nonlinear systems through the use of observed states. Our research also paves the way for the development of observer-based boundary control in robotics. The proposed control method could be applied to various soft robotic systems, such as inflatable beams and pneumatic mucles, to name a few examples. The theoretical results are substantiated by numerical simulations, which are further validated by real-world experiments conducted on a soft beam. The successful outcome of this research may be used to control the motion of a flexible marine rope, as shown in the accompanying video. Our initial analysis of 21 extremely distant active galactic nuclei, discovered with the help of a powerful near-infrared camera, revealed a range of features. Although we anticipated to see evidence of a continuous process producing the 21 micrometer emission in all sources, including a red shift indicator, this was not the case. Features in these objects were found to be similar to those observed in a group of less distant active galactic nuclei, and were often characterized by a flat spectrum. Unlike many more powerful active galactic nuclei at lower red shift, we do not see evidence of a separate less intense 21 micrometer emission in the data for these 21 objects. Despite expectations to see a red shift indicator in the data, this too appears to be the case. Although a separate less intense 21 micrometer emission has not been ruled out by the data, a more likely explanation is that this emission is simply a flat continuation of a less intense continuous process producing the 21 micrometer emission. This is in line with recent findings from studies of less distant active galactic nuclei. Additionally, a continuous process producing the 21 micrometer emission is consistent with the data in 19 of the 21 objects. Further examination of the data from a powder dust cloud, assumed to be similar to clouds in active galactic nuclei and the Milky Way, suggests that a continuous process producing the 21 micrometer emission is a more robust explanation of the data than a combination of emission lines. This is the first study to use a comprehensive code for simulating continuous processes producing the 21 micrometer emission in data from a powerful near-infrared camera to determine if a continuous process producing the 21 micrometer emission is a more likely explanation of the data in high red shift active galactic nuclei than a separate less intense 21 micrometer emission. This study presents a lightweight Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) prediction model, namely Lite-ProSENet, which demonstrates superior performance on multi-task datasets for prostate cancer. In contrast to earlier studies that focused on single-task datasets, this work tackles two challenging tasks - survival time analysis and classification - in a unified framework. The proposed model, built upon the EfficientNet backbone, is optimized for efficient prostate cancer prediction. The results show that Lite-ProSENet surpasses state-of-the-art models with notable gains, achieving a high area under the ROC curve of 0.8974 for classification and a strong Concordance Index of 0.817 for survival analysis. Notably, Lite-ProSENet's classification accuracy surpasses that of top-tier medical centers, indicating its potential as a lifesaving tool, along with its potential to be integrated into Electronic Health Records for enhanced clinical decision support. Moreover, the study showcases the effectiveness of feature alignment in boosting survival analysis results, as well as employing classification-task loss to enhance overall performance. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/JoeJiaochen/Lite-ProSENet for the benefit of the research community. The data used in this research comes from various public sources, primarily the Advanced Prostate Cancer and Metastases (APCM) study and the Metastatic Prostate Cancer (MPC) dataset. The model's efficiency, specifically its number of parameters, network depth, and computational cost, as well as its potential applications and weaknesses, are thoroughly discussed. The study finds that Lite-ProSENet, although lightweight, achieves remarkable gains over the original ProSENet model, emphasizing the value of carefully selected data for training. The effects of data selection on model performance are examined, and the study reveals that utilizing the APCM dataset alone yields a notable Concordance Index of 0.793. The study also delves into the integration of Lite-ProSENet with Electronic Health Records for enhanced clinical decision support, highlighting its potential to revolutionize the treatment of prostate cancer. The study closes by highlighting the merits and limitations of feature alignment, which significantly enhances survival time analysis in multi-task datasets, and concludes with the potential of Lite-ProSENet to save countless lives through early classification and guided treatment. The study's contributions to the field of prostate cancer prediction, as well as its broader implications for the research community, are meticulously presented. We employ a novel, highly efficient Fourier-Lagrangian local integration method (FLLIM) to integrate the nonlinear collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) system, enabling the construction of an accurate power spectrum from simulations with a high degree of precision. This innovative technique speeds up the integration process by at least 10 times compared to the traditional Eulerian methods. We utilize the FLLIM to simulate a universe of scale factor $a=1$ with a initial Gaussian field of wavelength $\lambda$ for $10^4$ to $10^6$ units, ranging from $\lambda \ge 0.1$ to $\lambda < 1$. The results reveal that the FLLIM method can accurately build a power spectrum with a high degree of precision across all scales, surpassing the capabilities of the Eulerian method. Furthermore, we observe that the highest precision is achieved at shorter wavelengths, while the error rate diminishes slightly at longer wavelengths. Additionally, we find that the most accurate power spectrum constructions occur at shorter linear initial wavenumbers, providing a highly reliable basis for analyzing the nonlinear evolution of the power spectrum. This new FLLIM method is an essential advancement for ongoing and future cosmological studies, offering a highly efficient means of simulating the nonlinear cold dark matter system and reconstructing an accurate power spectrum at all linear initial wavenumbers. Based on this promising progress, we are confident that the FLLIM method will yield similar successes in other related applications. As a supplementary tool for researchers, the power spectrum data constructed in this study is freely accessible at \href{https://github.com/HeLi-CAS/PSS-reconstruction}{https://github.com/HeLi-CAS/PSS-reconstruction}. Additionally, the FLLIM code has been made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/HeLi-CAS/FLLIM-code}{https://github.com/HeLi-CAS/FLLIM-code}. This paper proposes a deep learning-based approach to sentiment analysis of Arabic tweets. Our approach leverages the Long-Short-Term-Memory (LSTM) model, well-documented in the case of English tweet sentiment analysis. However, working with Arabic tweets poses distinct challenges, primarily resulting from the variations in spelling, grammar, and vocabulary usage. To address these challenges, we introduce an LSTM model integrated with a WordPiece model, similar to the one used in the Arabic BERT model. Our proposed model is put to the test on three classification tasks involving two datasets: the first dataset comprises 15k annotated tweets, while the second is the SemEval2013 image-related sentiment dataset. Our evaluations demonstrate that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across all three classification tasks, specifically 93% for the binary classification task, 89% for the quad-class classification task, and 90% for the Semeval2013 task. Our experiments also compare the performance of our proposed model against two other models: one based on LSTM with Word2Vec, and another based on CNN with different kernel sizes. Our results show that our proposed model outperforms these benchmarks, showcasing its effectiveness and generality in Arabic tweet sentiment analysis. Our source code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/mhanna97/Arabic-Tweet- Sentiment. Our experiments also highlight the importance of the model architecture, the dataset, and the pre-trained word embeddings used, serving as a guide for researchers to work with Arabic sentiment analysis. Our analysis also shows that the data sparsity continues to pose a challenge to the model's effectiveness, particularly when dealing with negative sentiment. Our proposed model, therefore, serves as a stepping stone for further research in this area, possibly informed by the advancements in the transfer learning-based approaches. Our additional contribution to the field lies in the manual handling of data sparsity through data augmentation techniques, specifically the generation of additional annotated data based on existing labels, and the modification of existing data. This relationship holds true for a wide array of starting points and shows no bias towards particular orientations. Furthermore, we explore how this complex system behaves under irregular conditions and examine the dimer's ability to maintain a steady speed when surrounded by an endless crowd, with their speed largely influenced by a critical area spanning one to three dimers. We also discover that their acceleration patterns in this steady state are consistent regardless of the crowd density but vary depending on the depth of this critical area. In addition, we examine their ability to maintain a consistent speed when surrounded by an endless crowd and investigate their behavior in multi-layer environments, with their ability to maintain a steady speed largely determined by the depth of the crowd in each layer and their speed in a single-layer environment. We then extend our analysis beyond dimer movements to more complex objects, such as triomers, and discover a surprising connection between their motion and the behavior of dimerizations in a cellular system. This study offers a significant advancement in our understanding of active movements within crowded environments and reveals fascinating links between their behavior and the features of more complex systems. Additionally, we showcase the remarkable simplicity of an effective model that can accurately predict the steady-state behavior of a complex system composed of 106 particles and demonstrate the remarkable precision of a statistical-based model in predicting the steady-state behavior of a complex system at the microscopic level. In doing so, we highlight an important connection between the stability of a system and the features of its constituent particles. Finally, we explore the potential of our findings and showcase the incredible potential of our study as a valuable resource for teaching students at the undergraduate level. Throughout our investigation, we encourage our readers to actively engage with our results by providing answers to frequently asked questions and inviting them to reproduce our findings using a simple code based on Sean's 'biology' package for Python. In doing so, we promote collaboration, transparency, and shareability among our readers. In conclusion, our study offers a highly original, thought-provoking, and inspiring research experience that encourages our readers to think creatively about the interconnectedness of complex systems. We then compare these results to those obtained from regular, random deployment methods, investigating the efficiency and validity of different deployment strategies in both heterogeneous and homogeneous networks. Wikipedia editors engage in editing to correct errors, improve clarity, and ensure neutrality, resulting in valuable insights into good writing practices. We leverage this editing behavior to enhance sentence quality labeling by pairing editors' feedback with machine learning models. Initially, human editors provide annotations on the quality of sentences in a small subset of articles, and a machine learning model generates annotations for additional sentences. Subsequently, a semi-supervised learning algorithm refines the labels using the edited articles, where sentences altered by Wikipedia editors serve as positive examples, and the original versions serve as negative examples. The approach can easily be adapted for other types of text modifications. We tested this method on 3,325 sentences from Wikipedia editors and found that combining editor feedback with machine learning models yields superior results, outperforming both human annotations alone and machine learning models without editor input. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating diverse editing behaviors yields high quality sentence annotations, surpassing the results obtained with a single type of edit. Ultimately, the annotated dataset can be utilized to improve sentence quality by informing models, guiding training, and serving as a baseline for evaluation. Moreover, the Wikipedia Editors' Feedback dataset presents a novel resource, allowing researchers to build upon and expand its capabilities, and offers a potential model for other Wikipedia contributors' feedback, and edits to other collaborative projects. This contradicted data drives the compression model to excel, resulting in superior performance compared to conventional distillation methods. By producing artificial labels that contradict those of the original model, DB3 achieves unique goals distinct from traditional knowledge distillation. Unlike other counter-black-box distillation methods, DB3 does not rely on an accurate pre-trained teacher; instead, it uses synthetic data generated from decision-making processes. As such, it is capable of adapting to various pre-trained teachers without requiring adjustments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DB3 can be utilized for compressing both classification and regression models, illustrating its broad applicability. Our experimental findings reveal that DB3 can successfully reduce model complexity while maintaining consistent accuracy for both image and text classification models. Notably, DB3's performance is often comparable to that of state-of-the-art distillation methods, all of which require collaborative training with a pre-trained teacher. We introduce a novel learning framework called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which enables two agents to learn behaviors mimicking each other without needing expert guidance or demonstrations. Through continuous interactive learning, the agents evolve whose actions resemble each other, promoting better understanding and interaction. By minimizing the difference in their behaviors, the system encourages both agents to perform optimal actions beneficial to both. Our theoretical analysis shows that under certain conditions, the agents will learn similar strategies, achieving a collaborative advantage. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of CoIL, demonstrating a significant improvement in both behavior imitation and mutual benefit compared to state-of-the-art imitation learning methods using demonstrations. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the similarity of agents contributes to better mutual benefit, providing valuable insight for future research in this domain. This paper examines the maximum likelihood (ML) decoding of convolutional codes through a sequential approach, using a cutoff rate based on the pairwise error probability, specifically the minimum of several cutoff rates related to different bias values. The study shows that, for any given bias, increasing the code length leads to a lower error probability, but a optimal trade-off can be achieved by selecting the best bias value. The paper also considers the average case, where the bias value is chosen randomly, and presents an upper limit for the average error probability in terms of the average crossover probability. Additionally, the paper compares the error probability performance of ML decoding with that of semidefinite programming (SDP) decoding, showing that, for long codes, ML decoding can achieve nearly the same performance, but with a significantly lower computational complexity. The experiments support a previous theoretical finding that ML decoding can reach near-capacity performance on the pairwise error probability metric. The results suggest that SDP decoding can be a good alternative to ML decoding for codes with short memory, but ML decoding may be more suitable for applications requiring low complexity and high reliability, especially when the codes have long memory. The experiments also indicate that SDP decoding can be less efficient than ML decoding on the pairwise error probability metric, but could be more efficient in terms of storage requirements, making it a good choice for such codes. The experiments further support a previous theoretical finding that maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding can reach near-capacity performance on the average crossover probability metric, using a crossover probability based on the minimum of several crossover rates related to different bias values. The results suggest that MAP decoding can be more efficient than ML decoding on the average crossover probability metric, but less efficient on the pairwise error probability metric, specifically by at least 0.18 dB for long codes. The experiments indicate that MAP decoding can be more efficient than SDP decoding on the average crossover probability metric, but less efficient on the pairwise error probability metric, specifically by at least 0.12 dB for long codes. The experiments further indicate that SDP decoding can be more efficient than ML decoding on the average crossover probability metric, but less efficient on the pairwise error probability metric, specifically by at least 0.06 dB for long codes. Recent research has focused on eliminating the need for time-consuming camera calibration when using depth sensors for robotic application development. Typically, depth cameras are used in a fixed position but often this isn't the case in practical scenarios. Our proposed method, Intrinsic Multi-scale Geometric Pursuit, estimates end-effector pose by integrating information from different scales and utilizing an error-backpropagation-like mechanism that corrects errors and updates estimates iteratively. To confirm the method's effectiveness, we conducted experiments using a depth camera mounted on a Universal Robot, demonstrating that our approach can generalize across various orientations without the need for calibration, achieving an average error rate of 3.69 cm after 100 iterations. Moreover, by integrating a depth sensor, our method can estimate end-effector pose more accurately than purely intrinsic-based approaches. All source codes and experimental data are available on our website.

In order to assess the level of interference within a wireless network, researchers employ a technique known as field measurement. By recording downlink traffic on a specific unit and analyzing it, they can determine whether neighboring units are interfering, as opposed to simply experiencing increased demand. A statistical model, specifically a binomial distribution, is used to make this assessment, at a specified probability level, when there is no interference. However, this method is affected by the choice of observation period and data collection units. Ideally, these units should be small and uncorrelated with each other. Typically, a network's physical boundaries, such as rooms or vehicles, are used as these units, as they are small and physically distinct. Nonetheless, selecting these units may not always be feasible or practical in various scenarios. As such, this research examines the effectiveness of alternative units, specifically bytes and seconds, in measuring interference and providing accurate results. By applying the method to a Wi-Fi network, consisting of 16 access points and 14 apartments, this study demonstrates the process of determining whether each apartment interferes with another, under different load conditions. Furthermore, we provide formulas to adjust the results for various packet loss rates, as well as derive a formula to estimate the probability of misclassification when there is no interference. These findings can be generalized to other networks, such as cellular and satellite networks, operating under similar conditions. Ultimately, this research aims to provide insight into the suitable observation periods, either per apartment or per network, for accurately detecting interference. A comparison between the proposed method and an alternative approach, based on the mean, is also presented, demonstrating the superior effectiveness of the method when the observation period is based on the network's physical boundaries. Additionally, we provide software to automate the process, facilitating the use of the method on any wireless network. Experiments were conducted to verify the proposed method's accuracy, using a real-world, medium-sized wireless network, operating at a specified bandwidth. Findings showed that the method's accuracy increased as the load decreased, reaching nearly 100 percent at low loads. Nonetheless, the method requires adjustment when packet loss rates are high, as this will lead to a higher than actual rate of false positives. Consequently, an adjusted formula is provided to estimate the probability of misclassification, even under high packet loss rates. Furthermore, research found that the level of packet loss impact on the method's accuracy varied greatly with different focal units, as opposed to a smaller experimental network, where the effect was minimal. Lastly, simulations were performed to evaluate the proposed method

A compound called [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$)$_2$ contains copper ions that are part of a specific type of geometry, allowing for magnetic fields to influence their properties in a unique way. This particular arrangement of the copper ions, surrounded by two specific organic molecules (pzt and 2-HOpy), creates an opportunity to explore the impact of magnetic fields on the material's overall magnetic properties. Under the influence of a strong magnetic field, the material's magnetic properties change in such a way that the magnetic correlations between adjacent copper ions in one dimension become suppressed, while showing potential for long-range magnetic order in a unique pattern known as a helical order, provided that an adequate amount of pressure is applied. A theoretical model has been developed to explain the observed patterns and how they change when subjected to a magnetic field, specifically through the use of a unique type of mathematical solution called the helical order parameter. This novel hysteresis-based model incorporates state variables that are updated in accordance with a set of rules, which leads to intricate behavior, along with a robust Hysteresis Index to quantify the randomness behind transient current fluctuations. Consider a group G acting on a metric space X, with a countable network, and let C_1(X) be the space of real-valued continuous functions on X equipped with the L^1 metric. We will show that the space A_h(X) consisting of G-equivariant non-expansive operators from C_1(X) to itself has a compact embedding if and only if the action of G on X is transitive. Moreover, if this condition is satisfied, we will provide a characterization of the compact embedding in terms of the orbit space O = X/G and establish that A_h(O) is isometrically embedded in C_1(O) with the L^1 metric. We will also investigate the embedding of A_h(X) in C_1(O) when the action of G on X is not transitive, and illustrate our results with various examples. Additionally, we will extend our characterization to the space A_c(X) consisting of G-equivariant compact operators from C_1(X) to itself. Our methods will combine those used in the study of G-equivariant probability measures and operator algebras. We will show that the space L^1(G,X) can be represented as a closed subspace of A_h(X), and that the space A_h(X) can be represented as a closed subspace of A_c(X). Our characterization of the compact embedding of A_h(X) will enable us to identify which group actions and metric spaces have embeddable non-expansive operators, and provide new insights into the equivariant non-expansive operators for previously studied spaces such as tori, spheres, and nilpotent spaces. Our work will unify and extend existing results in the field by illustrating novel connections between group actions, metric spaces, and the embeddability of non-expansive operators. The Einstein relation's validity can be assessed in non-uniform temperature systems. According to standard principles, the Einstein relation should be considered invalid. Nonetheless, in this letter, Einstein's relation is shown to hold for all time in systems with temperature gradients by utilizing Green-Kubo-type analysis. Additionally, the possibility of having both normal diffusion and tunnelling diffusion simultaneously is also demonstrated. These results are verified in a specific model representing a thermally biased particle in a box. It is found that the 'anomalous diffusion coefficient' and 'tunnelling coefficient' can be computed by utilizing correlation functions and by comparing them with the corresponding parameters obtained from Einstein's relation. These parameters are found to have the same physical meanings as their standard counterparts, thus providing greater insight into the system under investigation. Furthermore, the presentation offers an opportunity to introduce students to non-uniform temperature systems and the powerful tools of fluctuation dissipation relations for evaluating temperature profiles and as a means of exploring dynamic systems. These tools can be employed for either validating numerical simulations or as an experimental technique to measure thermodynamic parameters in physical systems. It is also hoped that this presentation will encourage others to utilize fluctuation-dissipation theorems as a means of exploring and understanding dynamic thermal systems. Moreover, this letter also serves as a platform to introduce a novel method for computing diffusion coefficients by utilizing operation counting, and by comparing it with the standard approach of utilizing correlation functions. Consequently, the presentation offers an opportunity for students to appreciate the fundamental 1st order importance of the fluctuation-dissipation relation in comparison with the second order Einstein relation. Finally, a means to experimentally validate diffusion and tunnelling coefficients proposed in this letter has also been proposed. This proposed method has potential for being employed both analytically and experimentally to investigate thermal systems. This research examines how different training heuristics in deep learning affect model characteristics. We specifically look at how regularizing the norm of model parameters influences representation complexity. Our analysis in various numerical experiments suggests that parameter norm regularization actually decreases the complexity of representations in contrast to common beliefs. Furthermore, we discovered that regularized models tend to have smaller diameter of activation patterns which might be a key factor in their improved generalization performance. To assess the reliability of our findings, we used multiple measurement methods of representation complexity, including a new one based on activation pattern analysis and a recently proposed approach involving random projection techniques. Our results are consistent across all these measures. We also investigated the effects of different hyperparameters of regularization heuristics and performed a thorough statistical analysis of generalization performance in high-resolution image classification tasks. Our study was conducted on the datasets of ImageNet, CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet with the help of ResNet, SeNet, and GNBN models of varying complexity. Our research identifies an optimal 'bend' point in the relationship between model complexity and number of layers, beyond which further increases in model depth lead to significantly degraded performance. We also developed two new diagnostic tools based on random projection and activation pattern analysis which help in understanding and explaining the effects of different training heuristics on generalization performance. Our work highlights the importance of formally defining and measuring model complexity in deep learning and motivates the need for more in-depth research in this area. Our implementation in TensorFlow is available at https://github.com/krhovnanov14/DeepNLM/tree/regulizarion-heuristics-level. Additional information can be found in the Supplement. Our work was partially presented at ICLR 2019 and the details are available at https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.01769v2.pdf. Our research was conducted at the Deep Learning Group at Czech Technical University in Prague, the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, the University of Berkeley, the University of Washington, the Microsoft AI Residency Program, the Google Deep Learning Course, and the ICLR 2019, in addition to various conferences and workshops listed at https://www.davidpolanicek.com/cv.html. A versatile technique for modeling particle decay processes has been developed, allowing for the precise determination of physical parameters such as the branching fraction, branching ratio, and time-dependent characteristics associated with flavor-changing neutral currents. This method leverages a unbinned maximum likelihood fit that incorporates the complete experimental data, thereby optimizing parameter estimation alongside calibration of experimental resolutions. Essentially, this approach treats the experiment's resolution as a free parameter, enabling the reconstruction of signal and background distributions through the simulation of observed data. As a primary illustration, the technique's applicability is shown in the analysis of $B^0_s \to J/\psi \phi$ decays utilizing LHCb experiment data. According to the results obtained, the values for $\mathcal{B}(\bar{B}^0_s \to \bar{B}^0_s J/\psi \phi)$ and $|\psi(m_\psi^2)|$ are $4.34 \times 10^{-6}$ and $0.0208 \pm 0.0009$, respectively. Furthermore, the method's potential limitations and areas for further improvement are identified within the context of emerging experiments. Lastly, a publicly accessible code for this analysis has been created and made available on GitHub for the convenience of other researchers. Specifically, the code can be accessed at the link: https://github.com/PaulOnufrijev/BsJpsiPhiUnbinnedMLCFIT.

To overcome this challenge, researchers have explored the potential of applying data augmentation techniques to expand existing datasets, thereby mimicking the effects of collecting fresh data while also incorporating expert knowledge. This research builds upon prior studies in which label augmentation and text transformations were applied to multiple-choice data to improve model performance. It expands upon this work by investigating the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques specifically designed for free-response data and composite items, which often feature essential contextual information. A comprehensive analysis of the findings from these studies demonstrates that effectively utilizing augmented datasets can lead to significant improvements in model accuracy and performance when grading essays, especially when employed in conjunction with model-specific training techniques. As a result, this research contributes to the development of reliable automated essay grading models and sheds light on the potential of data augmentation in educational data sets. Moreover, it underscores the significance of considering domain-specific constraints in augmenting dataset scales. Finally, it highlights the value of investigating novel, purpose-driven uses for pre-trained models and expert-knowledge-based data augmentation within the educational sector. By conducting an in-depth analysis of a comprehensive educational dataset, this study aims to evaluate and compare the performance of these two methods in the context of multinomial model. The distribution of opportunities within a society has an impact on the current generation's socioeconomic standing, which in turn influences future generations' opportunities and outcomes. Due to difficulties in empirically measuring opportunities, researchers often utilize a simplified model that attributes opportunities to the parents' socioeconomic status of the previous generation. This simple model suggests that opportunities are passed down through the parental lineage, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of disadvantage or advantage. However, the opportunities-to-socioeconomic-outcomes model faces challenges as parental socioeconomic status may not directly correlate with actual opportunities, leading to inaccuracies in policy insights and social equity assessments. This study proposes an alternative approach that uses a probability-emergent agent-based model grounded in network theory, replacing the traditional static model of opportunities. The new model represents opportunities as a dynamic interaction between agents within a network, allowing for opportunities to be distributed in a more diverse and dynamic manner. Additionally, the study uses a novel measure of opportunities to examine the effects of socioeconomic status on opportunity distribution and how this impact differs from the distribution of outcomes. Notably, the new model indicates that opportunities are concentrated in specific regions controlled by high socioeconomic status agents, creating a system in which opportunity distribution perpetuates the existing socioeconomic disparity. However, the study also reveals that opportunities can be altered by changes in the network structure, potentially enabling systems of shared opportunity to arise. Finally, the paper explores the practical implications of these findings for researchers seeking to utilize opportunities to inform social policies that can break the cycle of poverty and drive social equity. Ultimately, the study's insights can be utilized to develop and implement policies that not only address outcome disparities, but also strive to reconfigure the opportunity structure to benefit future generations. The study's code is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/Valerio-Fullini/Opportunities/tree/main. The DGN model can be found at https://covid19contacttracing.gnam.org/. The ABM code can be accessed at https://github.com/Valerio-Fullini/Opportunities/tree/ABM. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Additionally, the researchers would like to express their appreciation to the two anonymous reviewers for their feedback and suggestions. The phase factor that emerges when transforming the positions of identical particles, $\pi$, in Schrödinger's equation reflects the properties of the particles' spin. For particles with half-integer spin, $\pi$ is either +1; for those with integer spin, $\pi$ is -1. We have developed a simplified quantum walk model on a square grid, where particles with zero or unit spin move randomly, and their wavefunctions, subject to bounded boundary conditions, correspond to the eigenstates of the model. Our research involved manually calculating the eigenstates, and the resulting energy spectra, showing distinct groupings related to the sign factor $\pi$, are presented for square grids of various sizes, up to seven particles. Additionally, we have determined the transition probabilities between the eigenstates of the model. As a key outcome, the permanents of the transition matrices for one- and two-particle systems match the wavefunction-based permanent formulas proposed by Ambainis et al. and Ambainis et al., respectively. Furthermore, our model, particularly its large-scale behavior, appears to share connections with the permanent's representation as a positive semidefinite matrix, an important concept in operator theory. Our research also yields an interesting link between the wavefunctions of our model and the permanent of a matrix that describes random walks on a square grid. Our findings demonstrate that the wavefunctions, expressed as complex numbers, can be connected to the permanent's real-valued representation by normalizing with the volume of the square grid. Nonetheless, the resulting normalized permanent does not serve as the eigenfunction for bounded boundary conditions. Finally, our model may find applications in systems involving half-integer spin particles, such as the study of quantum liquids and related theories, as evidenced by an example involving two bosons exhibiting a sign factor $\pi = -1$. Our research may also open up avenues for research in this field, thereby enhancing our understanding of quantum mechanics through the integration of combinatorial ideas, particularly the permanent, into it. For instance, future studies could examine the relationship between the wavefunctions of our model and the permanent in the context of non-commutative probability theory, as well as the geometric interpretation of the wavefunctions, potentially revealing connections to the geometry of the square grid itself. Another area of investigation could be the analysis of the model under the persuasion of vectorized representation of matrices, as proposed by Harrow, sutton, and Grady in their paper 'random quantum circuits', as this concept could pave the way for novel algorithms and physical models

We introduce an innovative extension to RingCT technology, Delegated RingCT, 
  which offers two key advantages: greatly increased transaction speed and higher
  scalability. Compared to the standard RingCT protocol, Delegated RingCT cuts 
  transaction time down to a mere tenth of the original time, solely by 
  reducing latency. Furthermore, Delegated RingCT surpasses the current 
  RingCT capabilities by a factor of two to ten, in terms of transactions per 
  second, while maintaining the same level of security. To achieve these 
  achievements, Delegated RingCT introduces a two-tiered delegation system, 
  comprising a primary delegation level affecting the majority of users and a 
  secondary level influencing a smaller subset. Users can choose their level of 
  delegation to strike an optimal balance between anonymity and transaction 
  speed. Additionally, Delegated RingCT introduces a network scoring system to 
  prevent and deter malicious behavior, such as delegated ring size manipulation 
  and false delegation claims. To evaluate Delegated RingCT's effectiveness, 
  we successfully implemented a test wallet and assessed its proof-of-concept 
  through a series of transactions, demonstrating its practicality and the

Approximate solvers for linear systems, which find a feasible solution within a predetermined margin of error, have been shown to be polynomially complex and can be constructed using circuits of similar complexity. It has been conjectured that similar relationships exist for other combinatorial problems. To investigate this hypothesis, a class of derived problems is defined for approximate solvers, as well as for configuration problems, which are short linear systems, and it is shown that these derived problems can be expressed in terms of the complexity of the original problems. Furthermore, a set of lower bounds on the complexity of approximating shortest paths and maximum independent sets in undirected graphs is established, based on current bounds for these problems. It is also shown that approximate configuration solvers can be used to develop efficient circuit constructions for various combinatorial configuration problems. To demonstrate the hypothesis for configuration problems, a set of upper bounds on the complexity of approximating minimum spanning trees and maximum cardinality matching in directed graphs is established, based on current bounds for these problems. Additionally, a set of lower bounds on the complexity of approximating minimum spanning tree and maximum independent set in undirected graphs is established, which is shown to be close to the known upper bounds for these problems. While the hypothesis remains true for all the investigated configuration problems, it is shown that it does not hold for approximate solvers, as a set of upper bounds on the complexity of approximating minimum spanning tree and maximum independent set in undirected graphs is established, which is shown to be close to the known upper bounds for these problems. Their work established that the unit ball of ell_p has Qp-isometric dimension reduction properties for ε and p=2, but not for non-equivalent values of ε and p. This paper further explores Qp-isometric subspaces of ell_p and ell_inf and identifies specific spaces that cannot be reduced within ell_p using the Qp operator for certain values of ε and p. It also introduces a new dimension reduction operator Δp for ell_p and proves its uniqueness and efficiency in reducing the dimension of Qp-isometric spaces, as well as its applicability to all possible pairs of ε and p. However, this new operator does not provide dimension reduction for the same spaces that could not be reduced by the Qp operator. Ultimately, this paper concludes with new data on the dimension reduction of Qp-isometric spaces for p=1 and p=inf. This research demonstrates that the dimension reduction of these spaces can be achieved only when ε is a multiple of 1 or inf, respectively, in ell_1 and ell_inf, in contrast to the case of ell_2, where dimension reduction is possible for all ε. It also shows that the new dimension reduction operator Δp works for p=1 and p=inf, although it does not provide new results in these cases, and in addition, the paper notes some interesting differences between the dimension reduction of ell_p and ell_inf. In particular, it notes that ell_p is more easily reducible than ell_inf for small p, but ell_p becomes less easily reducible than ell_inf for large p, with a special case observed for p=3. To address this challenge, we present a innovative lifelong learning method called Hyperbolic Context-aware Continual Learning (H^2C^2L). This innovative H^2C^2L method effectively tackles key issues in continual learning, such as loss of plasticity during retrogression and parameter proliferation. It's noticed that negative degree-degree correlation enhances the maximum allowable error probability beyond the conventional belief-propagation threshold, due to the decoder's ability to efficiently correct more failures at higher error rates. Furthermore, we introduce a simplified metric to estimate the extreme-value approximation and also derive an upper limit for the connectivity gap through mean-field scheduling. It's observed that the proposed metrics yield accurate results particularly for protocols with repeated messages, thereby offering a precise belief-propagation threshold for such protocols. By applying the developed methods, we pinpoint the maximum tolerable error probabilities for certain belief-propagation decoding schemes, namely, quasi-cyclic, binary, and ternary LDPC codes, resulting in a 0.003-sigma enhancement over the conventional belief-propagation threshold. We also identify two critical factors that negatively affect the connectivity gap, namely, sparse connectivity and irregular distributions. Ultimately, we illustrate the relevance of our findings to information retrieval systems by providing an approximate belief-propagation threshold for erasure redundancy schemes used in such systems. This work proposes a Sequential Localization Multi-Particle Swarm Filter (SL-MPSF) method for nonlinear system tracking, incorporating safety constraints for linearized systems. The SL-MPSF algorithm divides the estimation process into two stages. Firstly, a preliminary location filter generates a coarse estimate through a particle swarm optimization, ignoring disturbances. Secondly, a localization filter produces a refined estimate based on the initial estimate and temperature from the first stage, while ensuring safety under disturbance conditions. The latter employs a heat-up scheduling approach to adjust a scalar multiple of the covariance matrix's eigenvalues proportionally to temperature. Consequently, this results in a Sequstart-like algorithm with bounded and disturbance-dependent scaling that remains adaptive and deterministic. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of SL-MPSF to within a bounded error of the true state, calculated as a function of initial covariance and system characteristics. The implementation of SL-MPSF demonstrates its capability to surpass unscentered PSO and MPSO counterparts in both convergence and stability, ultimately achieving significant safety and disturbance-tolerance enhancements. The safety feature allows for the incorporation of disturbance-bound contracts to maintain linear system safety, with practical applications in robotics and other field-related tasks. The proposed SL-MPSF outperforms conventional filters and particle filters in both performance and disturbance resilience, with key implementation details provided. The associated Matlab code can be accessed at the specified link. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of SL-MPSF in achieving superior convergence, stability, and disturbance resilience compared to its counterparts. The safety feature enables the incorporation of disturbance-bound contracts to maintain linear system safety, with applications in robotics and other related fields. The proposed SL-MPSF surpasses conventional filters and particle filters in both performance and disturbance resilience, showcasing its practicality and superiority. Language modeling has been the primary method for pre-training large datasets in NLP. Recent research suggests that large language models can achieve few-shot learning capabilities with high accuracy scores, often reaching performance levels comparable to task-specific fine-tuning with plenty of training data. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether low language modeling error is an effective indicator of a model's few-shot learning abilities. Our research targets this question by examining the connection between language modeling error, as measured by perplexity, and a model's few-shot in-context learning skills across a range of tasks. Our findings suggest no straightforward correlation exists between these metrics. Nonetheless, we identify a few key factors that can influence a model's performance in this area, including its overall size, the diversity of its training data, and the specific characteristics of the tasks it is attempting to accomplish. Our research implies that large-scale language models would be more effective if they were developed with a greater focus on the tasks they will eventually need to perform. Our findings are especially relevant given the growing interest in out-of-distribution generalization and few-shot learning capabilities among large language models. Galaxy clusters possess complex physics related to cold gas motion. A recent study by Gaspari et al. highlighted the significance of minor mergers as drivers of gas cooling and motion within clusters. Building upon this research, we investigate how anisotropic thermal conduction impacts minor merger outcomes. Our findings indicate that conductivity can slow down cold gas accumulation but enhance random motion. As a result, it accelerates gas dissipation and cooling, thus influencing cluster merger growth rates. Moreover, anisotropic thermal conduction can stimulate major mergers by cooling core collapse and facilitate minor mergers by driving cluster growth through surface brightness fluctuations. These findings have implications for understanding the role of thermal conduction in galaxy cluster evolution. Ultimately, they support the notion that minor mergers play a crucial part in maintaining cool core properties for large clusters. It is also possible that feedback mechanisms capable of counteracting conduction might be necessary for maintaining cool core longevity. It is hoped that further observations related to FUV emission related to the Chandra X-ray telescope and future missions like the LUKE mission will help to better understand the role of thermal conduction in galaxy clusters. \\

Keywords: galaxy clusters, cooling cores, conduction, mergers, galaxy evolution  \\
