We examine a significant MDP with 10,000 states and 10 actions, addressing both value and Q-function formulations, using the Grid World problem. By mapping the MDP's termination conditions to a matrix, we leverage the Generalized Minimum Residual Gradient (GMRES) method, a tool typically applied to linear systems, to iteratively solve the problem via policy iteration. The implementation of inexact GMRES enables us to compare its performance to the traditional exact GMRES. The study reveals that inexact GMRES requires about 5-7% more computation compared to the exact variant, while significantly outperforming policy iteration. Moreover, we achieve approximately 50-60 times faster computation compared to the exact GMRES method. Notably, the inexact GMRES approach allows us to tackle large MDPs with millions of states, representing a more realistic challenge in Reinforcement Learning. The PELUX library features the GMRES-based policy iteration method, accessible at https://pelux.github.io/. The Grid World problem used in this research is available at https://github.com/philiploper/grdwrl. Additionally, the inexact GMRES implementation has been deployed at https://github.com/philiploper/inexact_gmres. In contrast to state-of-the-art techniques in the field, such as Policy Gradients and Spanning Tree Consistency, the inexact GMRES method exhibits superior performance, requiring significantly fewer interactions with the environment. In particular, we achieve a 5-7% efficiency gain over Spanning Tree Consistency, while both approaches surpass Policy Gradients in terms of convergence speed. The presented results provide a foundation for future advancements in the design of efficient Reinforcement Learning algorithms. Furthermore, the study paves the way for the continued development and application of numerical analysis tools to tackle complex MDPs. Conversely, the study's findings could also inspire the creation of large-scale synthetic problems to facilitate the evaluation of future Reinforcement Learning methods. We examine weighted oriented graphs represented by $(G,\beta)$, along with the associated edge ideal $I_{(G,\beta)}$ within a weighted ring $S=\mathbb{K}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. We investigate when the ordinary and symbolic power sequences of $I_{(G,\beta)}$ equate, develop an criterion based on the weighted orientation's subgraph components to determine this equality, and further provide an approach to calculate the required parameters for oriented weighted bipartite graphs. Moreover, we introduce an indicator of the successful applications of this equality to certain graph orientations, namely $(G,\beta)$-Borel sets, describing their volume properties and establishing a one-to-one correspondence between such sets and prime ideals of certain type within $S$. We extend this indicator to certain graph substructures, dubbed $(G,\beta)$-Borel segments, and investigate their characteristics. Finally, we apply the developed tools to analyze the $(G,\beta)$-Borel sets and segments of specific orientable graphs, including those representing well-known mathematical objects, such as the Friedlander-Eisenbud construction and the Klingenfeder construction. Simulators are increasingly used to infer hidden states of complex systems, an activity known as inverse problems. However, certain issues arise when using simulators for inverse problems, such as multi-modality, non-linearity, the presence of uncertainty, and high-dimensional state spaces. To address these challenges, we present a method that involves modifying a conventional optimization-based simulator tuning approach to account for uncertain system parameters and produce a range of plausible state estimates. The proposed method utilizes a multi-objective optimizer to identify various parametric configurations that yield similar simulated outputs, effectively generating a sample set of probable system states. This sample set can then be refined through an inference analysis, producing a single post-determined state estimate along with associated uncertainty measures. The proposed approach is demonstrated to outperform a basic comparison method in a realistic study of power grid modeling. The developed methodology shows promise for addressing the intricate challenges of inverse problems in complex system modeling. The method is implemented in the PSAT power system simulator as an open-source extension, available at https://github.com/argonne-national-lab/psat-modular/ for use in future research and simulation efforts. The associated simulation data is archived at https://doi.org/10.11588/data.xf2/wc6344. WOS:000744509300001; SLAC Theses and Dissertures (OSU-2022). Reply to comment: We appreciate the comment from the editor and the feedback from the reviewer. We would like to address some of the queries from the reviewer as follows. Firstly, our proposed method does not necessarily produce a single optimal solution but rather a collection of state estimates corresponding to various simulator configurations, each with its own level of fitness. The sampling nature of our method is intentional in order to account for the inherent uncertainty in system parameters and model behavior. The proposed method can be modified in the future to incorporate advanced sampling techniques such as Latin hypercube sampling. Secondly, our method can be applied in various fields beyond optimization, and we hope the proposed approach will contribute to the continued growth and development of computer simulators and their various domain-specific implementations. Thirdly, we would like to provide a revised definition of our methodology's concept metric, which aims to quantify the level of fitness between simulated and measured outputs. The metric is known as the root mean square percentage error and is defined as the square root of the average squared difference between outputs, divided by the average absolute difference, multiplied by 100. The revised definition is as per the standard use of this error metric in the field

In this research, we investigate the robustness of learning from noisy data. Unlike traditional approaches, where assumptions about the data distribution can be made, we consider an even more challenging setting: there are no assumptions about the distribution. We focus on the influence of radius of the query and level of noise on data and develop strict bounds on number of data points required for distribution-free robust learning from noisy data. Our results demonstrate that these bounds are precise and nearly tight. Moreover, we show that these limits apply generally, encompassing any concept class. We also examine the significance of radius of the query and level of noise on data point generation and establish a theorem stating that distribution-free robust learning from noisy data is possible only when the radius of the query is small or the level of noise is small. As a byproduct of our research, we identify the smallest possible concept class for distribution-free robust learning from noisy data and provide a limit on the number of data points required for distribution-free robust learning when the label noise is 100% or pseudo Jaccard distance on data point generation is 1.5 or greater. Our research also offers an insight into why robust learning from clean data is often possible when the radius of the query is large, a phenomenon often referred to as 'hidden convexity.' We propose that one possible explanation for this phenomenon is that robust learning from clean data not only involves finding a distribution-free hypothesis that is close to all data points but also involves a hypothesis that closely resembles the data distribution, a challenge that is unique to learning from clean data. Our research also provides the first known bounds on number of data points required for robust learning from clean data. Our research examines how particle ratios vary as a function of centrality, where we analyze collisions from 7 TeV Au+Au and U+U as well as 54.4 GeV p+Au and p+p interactions. We observe a reliable trend of increasing particle counts with rising centrality, where the patterns of meson and baryon ratios mirror one another. As the scale of the collision system grows from small to large, we notice a shift towards equilibrium, with the hydrostatic model providing an insightful framework for understanding this phenomenon. We also investigate scaling relationships among ratios, such as K$/\pi$, $D/\pi$, and $\phi/\pi$, and discover that these quantities exhibit the same increasing centrality trends as a function of multiplicity in both Au+Au and p+p collisions. Our data, however, reveal a notable deviation from hydrostatic model predictions for these scaling relationships, where the observed patterns differ significantly from those predicted by string-based models. Where the hydrostatic model forecasts a distinct break in scaling behavior around $D/\pi$ ratios, the experimental data instead display a smooth, monotonous increase. Moreover, the fact that $K/\pi$ and $\phi/\pi$ ratios deviate from the hydrostatic model predictions more severely than $D/\pi$ ratios suggests that the hydrostatic model offers an increasingly accurate description of the collision dynamics as one moves from strange to charm quark species. Our research thus sheds light on the complex interaction mechanisms underlying high-energy collision phenomena, where the merging of quark and hadronic stages remains an unresolved issue awaiting further clarification. Lastly, we examine temperature-dependent interaction coefficients to derive a simplified elastic interaction time, which reveals an elastic interaction duration of approximately 2 GeV$^{-1}$ in both Au+Au and p+p collisions. Notably, our study uncovers no significant temperature variation in the strength of elastic interactions as the collision system scales grow from small to large. Our research thus provides a set of quantitative criteria that must be satisfied by any quantitative model of high-energy collision interactions. research on exceptional braided auto-equivalences, as well as offers a promising 
approach for future investigations. In an effort to facilitate clarity and

Estimating unobserved occupancy states is a critical yet complex issue in 
ecological research. Many current approaches are either restricted to small data 
sets or assume random associations between species and habitats. We present a 
Bayesian framework that doesn't have these limitations and can handle a wide 
range of detection probabilities, multiple observations from multiple survey 
methods, and variable characteristics of unobserved sites. This framework uses 
latent occupancy variables and incorporates prior knowledge about unobserved 
sites through their hyperparameters, which are adjusted iteratively using 
Laplacian Bayesian methods. We demonstrate the efficiency of this framework by 
analyzing real-world data from two distinct studies, one on bird species in 
grasslands and another on marine mammal species in the ocean. Our results show 
that this framework yields more accurate estimates of occupancy than other 
popular methods and also provides a confidence range for estimates that can 
be used for resource management and conservation. We find, for example, that the 
confidence intervals for our estimates suggest that Burrowing Owls are likely 
present in Montana but likely absent in North Dakota. Additionally, our results 
indicate that Virginia's estimated confidence range for the occupancy of Northern 
Aplomado Falcons includes zero, which means that the state's efforts to protect 
this species may still be insufficient. We advocate for a more comprehensive 
conservation strategy in Virginia and a re-evaluation of the species management 
plan in Montana and North Dakota. Our research shows that the Bayesian framework 
can offer crucial insights that may lead to species-specific research and 
conservation efforts. It can also be applied to a broader range of 
ecological investigations beyond occupancy modeling. We intend to use this 
framework in future studies to analyze multi-season observations, investigate 
species distributions, and explore other important issues in species ecology. 
Additionally, our research indicates that the efficiency of this framework can be 
significantly improved by incorporating geographical information about site 
characteristics. We plan to develop a new version of the framework that uses 
spatial correlations between sites to estimate occupancy more efficiently.

large data sets and can be used for detecting species occurrences in continuous 
environments. It will likely offer more accurate estimates of species detection 
probabilities than other approaches and will be an invaluable tool for identifying

This study introduces a correlation penalty term during the training process, promoting individual model parameters' unique contributions to the data without compromising the models' overall performance. Specifically, with the collaboration of Pan-STARRS1 data, our study obtained an optimal value of $73.12 \pm 2.64$ km/s/Mpc for the H0 parameter. Furthermore, the implementation of Gaussian Process regression on the residual variability demonstrates that there's no compelling evidence for a non-standard diversity at 95% confidence, but still yields beneficial results when incorporated into the reconstruction process. Despite low signal quality, they were able to confirm the presence of both neutral gas and ionized gas through multiple analysis methods. The mass outflow rates for neutral and ionized gas were approximately 3 times and 20 times smaller, respectively, than the star cluster's formation rate, signifying a significant reduction. Study findings reveal that the Carina's gas outflows slow down and switch from being primarily neutral to ionized around 10-100 million year age thresholds. It is anticipated that the newly observed outflows will contribute to the understanding of how star clusters interact with surrounding environments. Further research is needed to determine whether the detected outflows originated from the star cluster itself or the surrounding association. Additionally, researchers hope to verify the detection with additional, higher-quality data in the future. Furthermore, the study shows that the ionized gas outflows from Carina's star clusters exhibit similar properties as those observed in younger star clusters, suggesting a natural progression. It has also been observed that the detected outflows have lower velocities than those expected from common envelope interactions, raising potential alternative explanations such as outflow decay and external high-velocity gas interaction. The formation of global magnetic fields within rapidly rotating stars is often explained through the use of global circulation models, such as the bloated tachocline theory, in the boundary layer between the star's core and outer layers. These models typically assume the star's core rotates differently from its outer layers, resulting in a differential rotation boundary layer that drives a dynamo. Contrary to this notion, our three-dimensional simulations of a 1.44 solar mass, slowly rotating (P_star = 12 days) star with a strong magnetic field show that a global dynamos, including magnetic cycles, can and do develop even in cases of near-uniform rotation, using a procedure that generates global, laminar circulation patterns. These patterns, driven by the star's angular momentum distribution, have no connection with the presence of a tachocline and are instead characterized by slow, chaotic and three-dimensional fluctuations. These global dynamos, with magnetic cycle lengths of around 10-20 years, are found to be particularly vigorous when the star's core and outer layers rotate at similar speeds, resulting in a highly dynamic and three-dimensional magnetic field structure. Given the recently discovered prevalence of slowly and non-uniformly rotating stars among low mass stars, it's possible that global magnetic fields, such as those observed in stars such as CV Naos, could form in a similar way. Our study's results also raise questions about the established understanding of magnetic field evolution in these stars, as well as the broader field of stellar astrophysics.

Notably, our method excels in scenarios involving multiple input sources and outputs, achieving up to a 4% improvement in classification accuracy. McMini is a multi-core, native machine code model checker designed for efficient real-time operating system and multi-threaded software verification. Developed using C++ and CUDA, McMini utilizes GPU hardware to accelerate property checking, taking advantage of parallel processing capabilities. The model checker's core architecture is based on a finite state machine with edges representing machine code instructions, and incorporates tools like Coq for proof verification and Isabelle/HOL for interface management. Compared to other model checking solutions, McMini demonstrates substantial speed improvements, particularly in the verification of multi-threaded operations, thanks to its native machine code and multi-core capabilities. The model checker's efficient design also enables it to handle complex, real-world challenges. The source code is openly available on GitHub for public access and contribution. Misinformation spreading via social media platforms has serious consequences for individuals, communities, and society as a whole. In response, social media platforms are under pressure to develop effective solutions to mitigate the spread of false information. In an effort to address this challenge, WhatsApp launched a feature to label suspicious messages along with a warning message aiming to slow down the dissemination of potentially false content. To evaluate the impact of this feature, researchers analyzed a large dataset of messages consisting of both genuine and fake content, sent by users in Germany, to investigate the efficacy of WhatsApp's measures. Surprisingly, the analysis revealed that the labeled warnings had no significant effect on the spread of fake content. Conversely, the warnings appeared to have a counterproductive effect in some scenarios, prompting further investigation into the reasons behind these findings. To gain deeper insights, the researchers considered various factors such as the influence of group conversations, character limitations in messages, and the reliance on simple visual cues. By simplifying the design of the warnings and utilizing an effective testing framework, the researchers were able to design an experiment that confirmed the existing concerns. Based on these findings, multiple and tailored strategies were proposed to address the spread of misinformation on WhatsApp, including customizing group conversations, utilizing images, and implementing content-based classification techniques to identify and flag suspicious content. These proposed strategies could serve as a powerful tool in the ongoing battle against the spread of false information on social media platforms. This study examines the interconnection between commodity trading advisors and quick-reversing traders, identifying a possible win-win situation between these groups. Empirical analysis also shows that CTAs exhibit predictable trading patterns, which can be taken advantage of by short-term traders. A mutual benefit is suggested by the fact that CTAs' predictive characteristics enable them to generate superior performance when investing in certain trades, while short-term traders can capitalize on CTAs' predictable behavior by engaging in opposing strategies at key times. Moreover, it's observed that an advisory firm's trading style, specific market conditions, and individual trader experiences all impact the predictive behavior of CTAs, influencing their potential returns. Consequently, a strategy is proposed where an external expert assesses an CTA's predictive traits to set customized goals and reap better results. This study analyzed the coronavirus news coverage from a diverse group of US websites representing small and local media outlets. The researchers visited these sites on fixed dates in March and July of 2020, spanning a great diversity of states, cities, and rural areas. The aim was to examine the volume and the content of the local news coverage in response to the pandemic. The data collection process began with 398 sites, but due to technical difficulties in obtaining the July data from one platform, the actual count was 397. The main analysis focused on 292 sites that used WordPress. The research revealed a considerable variation in the volume of local news coverage. While some sites provided up-to-date information on the pandemic as early as February 2020, others didn't start until March and then mostly shared COVID-19 updates from state or federal levels, rather than local ones. The news content varied significantly across different geographic locations. Sites in densely populated areas focused more on pandemic updates from federal levels, whereas those in less densely populated areas focused more on local COVID-19 stories. The study also found that sites in areas with limited financial resources covered the pandemic extensively, often by relying on available technology and by adapting their existing workflows, rather than incurring additional expenses. In contrast, sites in more financially stable areas initially covered the pandemic extensively but later scaled back their COVID-19-related stories. The paper offers an in-depth examination of the local news media's response to the pandemic, providing insights that could help local outlets adapt to future global crises and continuing shifts in the societal landscape. The research also sheds light on the complex nature of local news coverage, influenced by factors such as the pandemic's impact, the financial constraints and resources availability, and the unique characteristics of the local media landscape in the US. The ability to generalize well beyond initial training data is a crucial property, especially when dealing with datasets from which we can generate an endless supply of counterfactual cases. A fundamental aspect of efficient policy learning algorithms is to count how many data points are needed for a particular level of performance and to accurately predict this number, allowing for scalable algorithm design. By utilizing the counterfactual policy, our research introduces a universal and absolute metric for measuring generalization, referred to as systematic extrapolation. This measure assesses an algorithm's ability to function without restrictions on its training dataset and without any limitations on its counters, making it highly relevant for algorithm design. We discovered that widely used upper bounds on generalization performance, such as margin and stability, are insufficient to guarantee even one additional generalization beyond the initial training data. We also established the existence of a set of highly generalizable algorithms with optimal performance and demonstrated that minimizing the distance between a classifier and its hard boundary is both a sufficient and optimal condition for achieving high-levels of systematic extrapolation. Our research highlights the crucial role of counters in facilitating scalable algorithm design and suggests the use of generative models as a viable solution for addressing generalization constraints in real-world applications. We further provide an empirical demonstration of the significance of systematic extrapolation in real-world settings and present the first algorithm to achieve optimal levels of generalization, according to our benchmark, in the tabular domain. Our research code can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/s4. Our research paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.11992. We hope that our research will facilitate a greater understanding of the relationship between generalization and counters. Additional information can be found in the supplemental material, at https://ramealex.github.io/s4. The Alexandrov embeddings of a normed space into its conical decomposition, introduced in relation to $l^p$ spaces with $p < 1$, were previously studied and found to be relevant in algebraic geometry's divisorial Zariski decomposition. This paper will explore their general form. By viewing an algebraic variety as a geometric object within affine space, updated insights into divisorial Zariski decomposition are now informed by metrics with certain curvature properties, drawing a connection between curvature and the positivity hierarchy of divisors. This connection is then used to demonstrate a method for resolving the positivity of a divisor on a variety with only terminal singularities by analyzing the Alexandrov body of a specific metric on the variety's coordinate space. This method is comparable to the minimal model program's method for resolving the exceptional divisors of a variety with only terminal singularities. Following this geometric approach, recent research findings on the connection between curvature metrics and algebraic geometry's positive-dimensional Zariski decomposition are now explained. This decomposition is then applied to calculate the Alexandrov body of a specific metric on the coordinate space of an abelian variety with a particular property, yielding a new characterization of abelian varieties with the property of being of general type and having a certain property related to their geometry. This method also allows for the resolution of the positivity of a certain divisor on a product of two varieties that satisfy certain conditions. Finally, recent research findings on the connection between curvature metrics and algebraic geometry's positive-dimensional Zariski decomposition are used to calculate the Alexandrov body of a specific metric on the coordinate space of a certain type of variety, yielding a new characterization of abelian varieties with a certain property, essentially a geometric variant of the Reinhardt conjecture. This method also allows for the resolution of the positivity of a certain divisor on a product of two varieties that satisfy certain conditions. In addition, certain results from the study of $l^p$ spaces with $p < 1$ are recalled and used to calculate the Alexandrov embeddings of a certain type of variety, yielding a new characterization of abelian varieties with a certain property, essentially a geometric variant of the Reinhardt conjecture. This method also allows for the resolution of the positivity of a certain divisor on a product of two varieties that satisfy certain conditions. Further research is needed to determine whether this method can be used to resolve the positivity of a divisor on any variety with only terminal singularities."

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to remarkable performance gains, particularly on simulated tasks like autonomous driving. Studies have explored transferring models directly from simulated to real-world settings, a concept known as sim2real transfer. This paper suggests redefining sim2real transfer and providing clarity on its interpretation. By separating performance into task and disturbance components, we identified that model transfer success is largely dependent on the disturbance component, often causing task accuracy to improve but disturbances to persist in real-world settings. This was demonstrated on the OpenFlightRoute dataset and in the 2020 URC challenge, where even highly accurate models exhibited poor transfer and distinct disturbance patterns in real-world versus simulated environments. To improve sim2real transfer, particularly in disturbances, we introduced a novel two-stage training method. Stage one involves training a model to minimize prediction errors and stage two incorporates online data collection and reinforcement learning to address the unique challenges encountered in real-world settings. Our method yielded significant improvements, reducing URC challenge stage two errors by 40% compared to the baseline and even surpassing the benefits provided by robustness- and uncertainty-aware models. Notably, our method proved adaptable to existing models and demonstrated broad applicability across various models and disturbances, as seen in autonomous driving and racing challenges. Overall, our research offers clarity on sim2real transfer, presents an innovative approach enhancing model performance and practical guidance on improving transfer efficiency between the simulated and real worlds. The proliferation of deepfakes poses an increasingly grave threat to society due to their rising veracity. As influence campaigns, propaganda, and manipulation increasingly harness the power of visually convincing multimedia content, its insidious impact on public opinion cannot be overlooked. Consequently, there arises a pressing need to develop reliable multimedia forensics that can detect and verify the authenticity of deepfakes. Although existing research focuses both correlation and learning-based approaches on identifying deepfakes, our analysis uncovers several crucial shortcomings, including the potential for false positives, inadequate generalizability, and the vulnerability to evasion attacks. In response, we propose an innovative counter-measure that combines the unique characteristics of multimodal information to enhance the robustness of deepfake detection. Specifically, a dual-stream CNN is designed to process video and audio separately, with an added attention module that prioritizes key features. Furthermore, we introduce two novel techniques - contrast enhancement and temporal alignment - to refine the disk-based distance metric, thereby significantly improving the robustness of our model against various attacks. Our proposed approach achieves exceptional performance on widely-used datasets such as UADFAD and Deepfake Dataset, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy of 98.76% and 97.14% respectively when compared to the existing literature. Moreover, our analysis via qualitative inspection and feature visualization reveals the efficacy of our model in identifying deepfakes, underscoring its potential as a reliable counter-measure against deepfake abuse. Ultimately, the code for our proposed approach is made available on our GitHub repository for reproduction purposes. Our proposed approach is described in further detail at https://github.com/jayjashn/Deepfake-Classification. As an emerging and dynamic field, we anticipate that our proposed methodology will contribute to the ongoing development of various counter-measures against deepfake abuse. Conversely, we also acknowledge the inherent risks and limitations inherent in leveraging machine learning-based solutions for high-stakes applications such as forensic evidence presentation. As a mitigating measure, we recommend that our proposed approach be utilized as a preliminary screening tool, complemented by the scrutiny of human domain experts to minimize the potential for errors and false positives. By taking a multi-faceted approach to deepfake detection, we hope to contribute to the evolving narrative in this field and look forward to the emergence of more sophisticated methodologies in the future. As an example of our proposed approach in action, an image depicting a fake interview from the UADFAD dataset is provided, along with our model's corresponding classification output. The atmospheric equilibrium models for temperate terrestrial planets surround their parent star, retaining heat captured from the star. These atmospheres are assumed to consist of multiple-layered components, separated by pressure levels, with gas exchange occurring through differential escape mechanisms. In contrast, planets with massive atmospheres or those that accreted gas giant cores are enveloped by a uniform layer of primordial gas, surrounded by a massive magnetosphere that controls gas loss through various escape mechanisms. A novel multi-component atmospheric circulation model is used, incorporating an advanced general circulation model capable of simulating both internal and external gravitational waves within these atmospheres. In particular, we examine the case of small, massive atmospheres, and discover novel atmospheric phenomena such as secondary circulation layers, distinct from cloud layers, that form on planets with sizes similar to that of Earth and develop a simplified framework for characterizing these atmospheres, depending on the planet's mass and size. In addition, we apply the new model to 1.6 and 2 times the mass of Earth-sized atmospheres, analyzing interactions between the atmosphere and a massive core, and find distinct effects on the atmosphere's thermal structure, compared to a model that accounts for core effects but not gas-core interactions. A new analysis of atmospheric properties and mass loss mechanisms for temperate and massive atmospheres is also presented, including a comparison with the recently proposed coupling between the core and the atmosphere in Ref. \cite{Rein2022}. We find an unexpected correlation between the atmospheric composition and the size/mass of the planet, and its relevance to bio-baseline studies of temperate and massive atmospheres, and explore the feasibility of sustaining liquid water on small and massive planets with sizes similar to that of Earth. A new prediction of the depth of the ocean on massive planets is also presented, based on the atmospheric temperature and size of the planet. Furthermore, we find an interesting contrast in the behavior of the carbon and nitrogen gases within small and massive atmospheres, and their potential impact on climate change studies, especially in regards to the size of temperate and massive atmospheres, and investigate the gas loss mechanisms in order to ensure that the ocean on massive planets remains liquid and to estimate the age of both types of atmospheres. The McCulloch-Pitts network, a model of discrete neural networks, has its foundations in the work of McCulloch and Pitts. Their work simplified the complex dynamics of neuronal interactions into a series of on and off states, representing either 0 or 1. This simplification allowed for the exploration of neuronal organization at a higher level, but it also limited the model's ability to capture finer details of neuronal activity. In contrast, the Hopfield network, a synaptically connected McCulloch-Pitts network, is capable of storing multiple patterns, although any initially stable pattern will eventually converge to a stable state. In an effort to increase the learning capacity of this network, researchers added noise to the neuron's activity, resulting in a distribution of 0s and 1s. This noisy network is now known as the Binary Gaussian Network (BGN) and has been found to be a reparameterization of the Hopfield network, bounded by its capacity limits. In an effort to increase the learning capacity of this network, researchers discovered a method involving a grid search and particle swarm optimization (PSO). This optimization algorithm uses a population of candidate solutions to locate and refine suboptimal solutions. In the context of the BGN, PSO successfully increased the learning capacity of this network, a refinement that can be utilized to improve the performance of machine learning algorithms utilizing similar neural networks, such as the deep Hopfield network. In contrast to traditional deep neural networks, the BGN and its deep refinements operate under binary constraints, making them more energy-efficient and easier to implement in hardware. As a result, the deep BGN presents a innovative model for binary neural networks, capable of adapting to complex tasks through optimization rather than complex architectures. Furthermore, this network model can serve as a versatile tool for teaching concepts of discrete neural networks to students at various levels of proficiency. Lastly, the code supporting this research is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository, located at https://github.com/nagashikamdeep/BGN-PSO. We examine a parameter-dependent system of polynomial equations and demonstrate how validated numerics can be utilized to compute individual branches of solutions. The key concept employed is the verified continuation method, which is an extension of the verified Newton-Raphson method for solving absolute or relative perturbation problems. By incorporating an validation process for the solution set of a guide polynomial, we are able to stay within an accurate box that contains an isolated branch of solutions. The technique is illustrated with two examples, including a problem of geometric phishing in relation to control theory and another involving elliptic integrals, both of which leverage the arithmetic of algebraic numbers to verify solution branches. Our findings are even more versatile and can be applied to non-polynomial systems, as long as an equivalent polynomial model is present. The paper concludes by discussing potential future directions for further research. These ideas have potential applications in a variety of fields, including physics, biology, economics, and engineering. Further study is also planned to explore the connection between the complex analysis of polynomial equations and the real solutions that can be found using the verified continuation method. Additionally, future research aims to develop an efficient algorithm for determining the connectivity of solution branches, as well as finding proof certificates for complex analytic properties of these branches. Finally, future research aims to apply and extend the verified continuation method to parametric geometric and topological deformation problems. de novo, as well as to existing issues in field research. 

The conceptual framework discussed in this research was initially presented in an earlier paper, but the present paper provides an expanded and refined explanation of the ideas presented there. In particular, the verified continuation method has been reworked to eliminate any dependence on symbolic computation, as well as the associated issue of combinatorial explosion, by utilizing algebraic models of polynomial equations and the arithmetic of algebraic numbers. The presentation in this paper is primarily drawn from research completed in 2021, with the exception of the geometric phishing problem which was added in 2022. Earlier versions of the material presented in this paper were presented at the respectively 2021 and 2022 International Symposium on Symbolic Computation, however the current paper includes significantly refined and extended presentations of the material presented there.

By looking at the ages of these star clusters within or surrounding these galaxies, we determined that the star formation occurred over a relatively short period of around 1 billion years in Encaladus and around 2-2.5 billion years in LMS-1. Our results also indicated distinct star formation patterns for the blue-halo populations associated with these galaxies, suggesting they were likely triggered by the interaction that led to their destruction as dwarf galaxies and subsequent merger into the Milky Way's blue-halo population. We discovered that the star clusters surrounding Encaladus formed before and after a critical event in the galaxy's history, likely related to its interaction with the Milky Way, while the star clusters surrounding LMS-1 formed primarily around the event and subsequently contributed to its destroyed as a dwarf galaxy and subsequent merger into the Milky Way's blue-halo population. We initially predicted a age range of 8-10 billion years for LMS-1 based on its metal content but found the star cluster's age range to be inconsistent with that result, suggesting further research is needed to understand this galaxy's star formation history. Our research supports theories that the destroyed dwarf galaxies Encaladus and LMS-1 merged into the Milky Way's blue-halo population around 8 billion years ago in the form of multiple substructures. Affective annotations are costly to acquire. Even with the use of selective labeling techniques, where only a subset of cases is labeled, data preparation becomes time-consuming and often slows down machine learning model development. This paper proposes a novel method to automatically generate annotated cases while utilizing selective labeling. This method leverages a generative model in a multi-task setup that simultaneously generates both labeled and unlabeled case outcomes simultaneously. Our experiment demonstrates that this method excels at outcome prediction but struggles with generating accurate annotations for complex data sets like emotions. This study highlights the challenges of applying deep learning-based automatic annotation techniques to real-world, emotionally rich content. As a result, we recommend against using this method for domain-specific applications like affective computing. Instead, this research serves as a basis for future investigations into the automatic annotation of affective data. We establish a version of Borel Wadge determinacy within the context of second-order arithmetic with strong $\Sigma^1_1$ induction, which corresponds to a fragment of reverse mathematics known as PTAE^{\leq\omega,1}_1. This determinacy concept is equivalent in this setting to a strengthened form of uniform Borel Wadge determinacy. Furthermore, it is known that this form of determinacy exceeds the determinacy of uncountable linear orderings, as well as true second-order arithmetic, within the same framework. Additionally, it is proven that not all models of arithmetic satisfy Borel Wadge determinacy, as this concept is equivalent in this setting to a strengthened form of projective uniform boundedness, which cannot be derived from cut-free arithmetic. Finally, it is proven that projective uniform boundedness holds in any model of arithmetic that is arithmetically universal for a certain class of models, which includes the well-founded part of any non-well-founded model of arithmetic. Consequently, Borel Wadge determinacy also holds in such models. All existing high-level proofs of Borel Wadge determinacy within reverse mathematics have employed a form of quotient transfinite induction; however, in the current work, it is shown that this concept can be derived without resorting to such an induction without sacrificing $\Sigma^1_1$ induction. Instead, a novel concept known as quasi-induction is employed, which is proven to be sufficient for this purpose. Quasi-induction is then further characterized and its relationship to other concepts established within the framework of PTAE^{\leq\omega,1}_1. Current methods for training pruned neural networks assume an equally pruned model for both training and inference, to ensure accuracy matches the number of active parameters. However, this equal pruning approach leads to over-pruning and inefficient resource use, particularly in convolutional layers. To address this issue, we present ClickTrain, a novel method, to efficiently train pruned neural networks, by dynamically determining the degree of pruning for both training and inference models based on their structure. ClickTrain achieves significant gains over state-of-the-art pruning methods, reducing pruning rates while maintaining accuracy, resulting in a more efficient model architecture with minimal computational overhead. Additionally, ClickTrain enables the creation of highly accurate and efficient models for image classification, yielding a superior balance of performance and efficiency. Our results show ClickTrain outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with a 1.0% accuracy drop and 19.1% speed-up, or a 3.0% accuracy drop and 34.1% speed-up, when compared to the original unpruned model. Furthermore, ClickTrain's designs and findings provide actionable insights for future pruning studies. We provide an overview of algebraic and relational approaches to substructural modal logic and define duality theorems for specific frameworks. We then establish a duality theorem for a particular framework of substructural modal logic and explain how it applies to existing theorems within the field. We also introduce the concept of a relativized Kripke model for substructural modal logic and demonstrate that every relativized Kripke model can be represented by a corresponding algebraic model. Additionally, we identify modal logics that correspond to both the algebraic and relational approaches within the broader family of substructural modal logics. We conclude by highlighting potential areas for further research within the field. Despite the extensive research on substructural modal logic, there remains a significant gap in understanding how the concepts of relativization, duality, and correspondence relate to each other. As a result, the hope is that this work will serve as a useful point of entry for researchers interested in substructural modal logic and its various extensions. We briefly address some of the existing limitations of our framework and mention a few relevant areas of ongoing research. Specifically, we note that while our work focuses primarily on the algebraic and relational structures, there is also a growing interest in the geometric and hypersequent-based approaches to substructural modal logic. We also recognize that the topics of relativization, duality, and correspondence are not exhaustive and may be applied to further variants of substructural modal logic in the future. Lastly, the work mentions that the framework of substructural modal logic offers a versatile setting for exploring various notions of axiomatic validity and associated proof systems, thus enabling the possibility of novel contributions in this area. The merger of two compact stars provides a extraordinary opportunity to observe a singular cosmic event across various wavelengths of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation.  Observations of low-frequency gravitational waves through secondary beat frequencies may be examined simultaneously with high-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted in the initial stages of the merger.  We investigated the feasibility of observing simultaneous gravitational and electromagnetic radiation from a compact object merger that occurred in a black hole remnant.  Our analysis focused on two neutron star combinations, NS1854950612 and NS-4, which yielded distinct fiscal and electromagnetic characteristics.  Our simulations predicted that observing the 91 Hz gravitational wave from the first neutron star combination could be concurrent with ultraviolet and optical electromagnetic radiation from the 181 Hz secondary beat frequency.  Nonetheless, the 149 Hz gravitational wave from the second neutron star combination failed to coincide with its corresponding 297 Hz secondary beat frequency in electromagnetic radiation due to insignificant amplitude of the latter signal compared to background noise.  Ultimately, direct visual observations of both types of radiation will be essential in enhancing our comprehension of neutron star mergers and their numerous astrophysical implications. In complex decision-making scenarios where multiple objectives are involved and rewards are discrete, finding an optimal operational policy can be challenging due to the large space of policies and the difficulty in exploring them effectively. To overcome these difficulties, a new algorithm has been developed that utilizes a primal-dual approach and latent variable mapping to identify a desirable policy for maximizing cumulative rewards in a multi-step decision-making environment with dynamic changes. The algorithm's effectiveness has been proven through a theoretical analysis showing its convergence toward an optimal policy, and its practical benefits have been demonstrated in practical problems such as controlling a sequential game through action encouragement and optimizing traffic assignment by distributing rewards. The results reveal that the algorithm outperforms existing methods, including multi-objective reinforcement learning and dual free methods, in these applications due to its capacity to incorporate additional constraints and achieve convergence without relying on a stopping criterion. The algorithm's execution speed is also comparable to or faster than these existing methods, with a notable improvement of up to 10 times in the traffic assignment example. The theoretical analysis underlying this algorithm's convergence involves bounding the variance of its policy, L, and latently mapped variables, Z, by analyzing their relationships and properties such as smoothness and duality gaps in optimization problems. By showing that the algorithm's policy achieves a trade-off between exploration and exploitation, the complexity of which is dependent on L's dimensionality and the algorithm's sample complexity, a new framework has been developed for studying the algorithm's efficiency and scalability. The algorithm has been further evaluated in a study of sequential games involving 10 to 40 agents across various university campuses, where it demonstrated an average convergence rate of 0.95 and 0.987 for respectively encouraging actions and reaching a Nash equilibrium in comparison to 0.927 and 0.966 for multi-objective reinforcement learning and 0.947 and 0.958 for dual free methods. To promote the algorithm's usability, an open-source implementation has been provided for other researchers to test and evaluate the algorithm in various applications. This research formalizes the BPS state counting problem from a moduli space perspective, particularly focusing on the degeneracies of particles in twisted localized vertex operators on the Hilbert scheme of $C^2$. By leveraging the Fukaya--Ono duality, it is demonstrated that the degeneracies of BPS states can be represented as the exponential growth of indices from the twisted localized vertex operators, thereby establishing an duality between the Fock space and the bounded cohomology of the Hilbert scheme. Furthermore, it is discovered that the degeneracies from twisted localized vertex operators exhibit exponential growth with $K$-index growth, where $K$ represents points on the Hilbert scheme, thus resolving the BPS state counting problem through this duality framework. Computations of degeneracies also show logarithmic corrections and asymptotic dominance by one-player games, verifiable against known results including Nekrasov and Shaginian's work. Lastly, dualities to Hermitian Yang--Mills equations and instanton counting are explored, examining the growth of degeneracies and spectral gaps as the Hilbert scheme's $K$-index increases. It is observed that BPS state counting, instanton counting, and Hermitian Yang--Mills equations are mutually equivalent in this context, exhibiting continuity across the spectrum. Ultimately, this research provides a general framework for counting BPS states, applicable to any symmetric orbifolds, utilizing the exponential growth of degeneracies' behavior as the orbifold's 'index' grows. This framework could potentially be extended to other geometric invariants, like Gromov--Hausdorff, Gromov--Witten, and Donaldson--Barretti invariants in the near future. Additionally, it explores Hermitian Yang--Mills equations and the topological vertex formalism as complementary methods for calculating BPS state degeneracies. Due to technical constraints, this research only examines degeneracies of particles in twisted localized vertex operators on the quintic 3-fold as an example case for the Gromov--Hausdorff, Gromov--Witten, and Donaldson--Barretti invariants. Nevertheless, it is hypothesized that the degeneracies of BPS states can be represented as the exponential growth of indices from the twisted localized vertex operators for any geometric invariants, potentially uncovering new aspects of these invariants, as seen in the quintic 3-fold's asymptotic dominance by one-player games. Epidemic spreading in complex networks is influenced by various factors, including network structure and disease characteristics. Researchers have been able to predict and analyze epidemic spreading with considerable accuracy in some networks, but this prediction becomes increasingly difficult in other, more complex network configurations. To shed light on this variation, we studied and compared the predictability of epidemic spreading in networks with different degrees of complexity. By analyzing extensive numerical data, we found a strong correlation between network bridgeness and the ability to predict epidemic spreading. Specifically, our analysis revealed that networks with robust structures allow for precise prediction of epidemic spreading, particularly when the infection rate is low. In contrast, our results show that the accuracy of predictions decreases for networks with fragile structures or high infection rates. To provide theoretical validation for these findings, we developed a mathematical model based on network clustering, which effectively predicts the accuracy of predictions for various network configurations. Our comprehensive analysis highlights the importance of network structure in predicting epidemic spreading and can inform predictive modeling for different network configurations. Furthermore, our research may be applied to other processes that spread through complex networks, such as information dissemination. An additional study on predicting epidemic spreading in evolving networks has been submitted under the title "Predicting Epidemic Spreading in Growing Networks". [An accompanying paper is also being submitted as "Evolving Network Predictability: Factors Affecting the Accuracy of Predictions"].

A significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) lies in its tendency to violate critical safety protocols. Current methods often employ constraint violator detection and correction mechanisms but do not guarantee the elimination of all violative actions. Violations can prove costly, even when slightly modified actions adhere to the set limits. Techniques such as penalty functions also fail to guarantee the avoidance of violative actions. In an attempt to address this issue, we propose using a bi-level RL method. At the top level, we collect and store historical constraint violator actions and train an action prediction model using these experiences. The model is trained to identify the most likely violative actions and their corresponding probabilities. At the bottom level, we integrate this model into the original RL problem by incorporating it as both the reward function and the dynamics model. This approach guarantees that all generated trajectories in the roll-out phase adhere to the set limits. In addition to ensuring the safe deployment of RL agents, our method also reduces the exploration expense by eliminating unnecessary exploratory actions predicted to violate the set limits. Experiments conducted on two complex systems - a 3D quadcopter to avoid a spherical area and a storage system to prevent overloading - showcase the effectiveness of our method. Firstly, it guarantees the complete avoidance of violative actions. Secondly, it achieves comparable performance to the violator detection method without dynamic model augmentation, indicating the potential for increased reward by eliminating violative actions predicted by the model. Thirdly, it significantly increases the safe deployment of RL agents compared to the violator detection method, indicating the potential for reduced exploration expense by eliminating unnecessary exploratory actions predicted by the model. In addition, our method demonstrates the potential for increased safety and reduced exploration expense while achieving the safe deployment of RL agents. We present a distributed control system comprising of a centralized controller and module-specific controllers working in tandem, allowing a group of mobile robots to collaboratively navigate their environment through learning-based control strategies, even in the absence of a global map. Our layered control system empowers these robots to adapt their movement via sensing data collected from their local environments. Our research highlights the effectiveness of this distributed control approach in group navigation using multiple mobile platforms equipped with sonar sensors as demonstrated through an experimental analysis. Additionally, the robustness of our layering technique is validated by its ability to withstand disruptions to individual module controllers without impacting the group's overall performance. Our open-source framework and experimental results are made available for the purposes of documentation and replication. This work is inspired by the social behavior of ant colonies where robots following a set of pre-defined rules resulting in a navigable group even in the presence of disruptions. Similarly, our distributed approach draws parallels to the design of self-healing systems, also our research shares similarities with stochastic sensor navigation. Furthermore, we pose an energy-efficient navigation problem as a challenge. Our solution is based on the principles of co-evolutionary learning, where two groups of mobile robots - leaders and followers - take turns adapting their movement via sensing data collected from their local environments. As a result, an effective centralized controller is derived from an evolutionary process, where the best fitness scores are obtained by minimizing confusion between robot groups. We present new observations of Nereid, a moon of Neptune, derived from a study conducted using the WISH instrument on board the ARIEL satellite. This study provides Nereid's first high-resolution spectral map in the 1.1-5.0 $\mu$m spectrum. It was based on a combination of Nereid's brightest occurrences between 2002-2007 and a signal collected in 2019. This spectral map indicates significant absorption patterns in Nereid's surface features, most notably a prominent absorption of about 40% at the 3.0 $\mu$m region, which suggests the presence of methane ice. This is complemented by a discovery of a weak signal indicating the presence of fresh tholins, likely resulting from methane catabolism, at wavelengths of around 2.9 $\mu$m. Using detailed modeling, researchers found that two surface features, designated as $\sigma$ and $\tau$, effectively replicate the observed spectral patterns. Analysis of the data suggests the presence of methane ice particles between 40 $\mu$m to 120 $\mu$m in size, dominating Nereid's surface, as well as smaller particles, approximately 5 $\mu$m or less, contributing to the absorption patterns. This study provides significant insights into Nereid's composition, providing the first direct evidence for methane ice on a moon other than Triton. Compared to other outer solar system icy bodies, Nereid's surface appears to have distinct characteristics. This research may be used to interpret future observations of other moon-satellite systems, particularly those in the outer solar system. Additionally, it paves the way for a new generation of computers to conduct numerical simulations focused on Nereid's thermal evolution, which could help to better understand its color patterns. These simulations could be based on an advanced generate-and-test algorithm that produces surfaces featuring anomalous blue colors, resulting from the thinning of a frozen methane layer. This could be a new method to create artificial, moon-like surfaces featuring unique colors. Additionally, it could be used to investigate how the moon's blue colors, which decrease with distance from the center, come about through the interaction of a blue color-producing layer and a frozen methane layer. We analyze projective planes resulting from the projection of affine planes, where these affine planes are defined over a ring, and we identify specific conditions under which a projective plane can be formed. Additionally, we derive conditions under which a projective plane can be non-descriptive, and we examine exceptions to projective planes constructed in this manner. Furthermore, we investigate subplanes of projective planes and their relationship to rings, and we discuss projective planes comprising units of a ring. Lastly, we study the uniqueness of projective planes arising from specific ring configurations. Moreover, we showcase examples of projective planes that can be described using a simple mathematical concept known as a quadratic form. We also explore horospherical projective planes and their connection to rings. Hq-projective planes have recently been shown to have an interesting property: for rings with a specific mathematical property called Hq-irreducibility, a simple description of a quadratic form can imply the projectivity of the resulting plane. As a result, we now have a more powerful tool for creating projective planes, allowing us to construct new projective planes. For example, we can create a projective plane of order 127 using a specific ring, which is the first plane of its kind to be described using a simple mathematical concept known as a quadratic form. We also show that many of the projective planes we have been studying are actually isomorphic to planes that can be easily constructed using standard mathematical techniques. However, the relationships between different configurations of states remain unclear. We also show that equivalent configurations have equivalent implications for nonlocality and contextuality, as well as equivalent roles in ontological frameworks, preserving their underlying physical properties. We demonstrate the versatility of our formalism by applying it to compound systems, then illustrate its applicability to essential resources in Bell/Maydeu-Sliwa contextuality and nonnonlinearity, before finally addressing its limitations. Our work provides a unified approach to analyzing state configurations, offering a valuable tool for further research in the field. Our findings may also be accessed through a dedicated interactive platform. In this study, we demonstrated the validity of the generalized Riemann hypothesis for all finite fields with characteristic p, a concept previously explored by David Bourgin. Furthermore, we established a functional equation analogous to the Polya theorem for  p-adic solenoids. To accomplish this, we employed continuous functions with compact support on the p-adic solenoid. Additionally, we formulated an analog of the Polya theorem for  p-adic solenoids. Conversely, we proved a functional equation for the L-function of the group of units of the ring of integers of the field of  p-subfields of degree 2 relative to Q. By utilizing our results, we solved a critical problem related to the functional equation and its connection to the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Finally, additional applications were identified. Schematic representations of  p-adic solenoids can be visualized as flows in compact spaces, and we proved a functional equation for the L-function associated with these groups, a concept previously explored by Michel Verbitsky in the case p = 2. Key contributions of this study include the resolution of a critical challenge, as well as additional  p-adic geometric generalizations of the prime geometric divisor conjecture. It is worth noting that these findings are highly likely to be true but cannot be proven using current mathematical techniques. Extensive technical additions were incorporated to ensure the clarity and understanding of our study. These technical additions hold independent value and may be useful in future studies. Finally, based on our findings, we provided a geometric generalization of the prime geometric divisor conjecture for  p-adic solenoids as well as for certain related groups, a concept previously explored by Richard Baker, Lior Fishman, and Florian Strungmann. Additionally, our study offers an independent verification of their work, in addition to providing a connection to the work of Michel Verbitsky, discussed earlier. This paper introduces a novel, universally applicable structure for computing salient object detection in color and depth images. It integrates multiple color image processing techniques at once, streamlining computational efficiency by utilizing a single universal block. Additionally, the method incorporates a depth-induced saliency map and a collaborative fusion module that enhances the salient object detection with both color and depth cues. Notably, the framework can be adapted for RGB-based input by omitting the depth module, making it a versatile tool for a range of image processing tasks. Extensive empirical tests demonstrate the outstanding performance of the proposed structure, achieving state-of-the-art results on various salient object detection datasets and rivaling existing methods with its efficiency. This paper presents Sys4, a system that participates in the 2019 JCDT abusive content challenge. We focus on detecting English tweets that may contain hate speech. We developed a two-stage classifier composed of an annotation-based filter and a neural network classifier to tackle this task. The first stage utilizes an annotation database created from the training data to identify specific labels, while the second stage employs a neural network to handle remaining data without labels. We designed our model to be efficient by reducing processing time for classification. We used the BERT pre-trained language model to enhance our performance on the JCDT dataset. We evaluated our system through an external test and achieved a macro F1 score of 75.32% for detecting abusive content, outperforming the baseline score of 71.00%. Furthermore, we ranked 4th out of 11 competing systems with a macro F1 score of 75.32%, while first place achieved a macro F1 score of 77.96%. Despite not quite securing the top spot, we successfully applied the JCDT dataset to validate our system's effectiveness through an external test. The dynamic memory management of GPUs is a delicate operation due to the need for manual memory allocation and deallocation on the GPU device. Current solutions, such as CUDA's malloc and free functions, have significant drawbacks including prolonged memory waiting times and data transfer losses between the host and device. In ideal scenarios, a memory allocator would eliminate data movement and provide efficient memory management by directly accessing the GPU's memory pool. The DynaSOAr is the first advanced GPU memory allocator designed for CUDA environments to efficiently handle memory allocation and deallocation operations on the GPU device. By utilizing a tree data structure, DynaSOAr optimizes memory allocation and improves performance through splitting, merging, and balancing techniques. The algorithm relies on a best-effort approach to free memory blocks when possible and relies on the GPU's memory pool to handle cases where memory cannot be recovered. Comprehensive benchmarks conducted by DynaSOAr show substantial improvements over the standard CUDA allocator, such as increased throughput of 3.45 times and reduced runtime by 2.31 times, in various scenarios including scientific computing, data compression, and other general GPU computations. The robustness measures described are useful in two ways: they enable researchers to identify decision functions that perform well despite changes in environmental conditions, and they facilitate a more accurate assessment of a decision function's potential when its preferences are affected by uncertainty about the characteristics of its input instances. To illustrate the utility of these measures, they are applied in a variety of scenario-based decision-making problems. Ultimately, the research presents a new method for evaluating decision functions in uncertain environments and showcases its practical applications. Applying this method to the CMZ, made up of anisotropic density patterns at large scales and semi-spherical structures at small sizes, we find that their density structures become increasingly circular as we zoom in. We examined how electron spreading influences non-linear absorption modifications at high intensities in metallic nickel. Utilizing ultra-fast X-ray absorption spectroscopy with 120 femtosecond pulses, we observed substantial changes in the near threshold absorption of 898 eV X-rays. These observations indicate a rapid increase in absorption as the electron cloud transfers energy from a smaller to a larger area, reducing the effective threshold energy. Through comparative studies of theoretical models, we found that in nickel, changes in plasmon energy dominate the linearity of absorption modifications. Consequently, non-linear effects are largely dictated by the increase in absorption as the electron cloud expands, causing the threshold to shift to lower energy levels. As number of Internet of Things (IoT) devices grows, so does concern over their potential misuse. Accurate classification of IoT devices is crucial for preventing and detecting cyber attacks, but often faces challenges due to the limitations of mirroring systems and unknown device behavior. Currently, classifications in security labs are based on basic characteristics and limited resource allocation, but in real-world scenarios, classifying a device within a short period of connection is essential. Given the constraints, misclassification becomes inevitable, but what level of risk is acceptable? To address this, a cost-aware classification approach using expected risk is presented, where the cost of accurate classification is compared to the cost of false classification to determine acceptable misclassification rates. However, in contrast to standard expected risk models, this approach takes into account both the cost of accurate classification and false classification, rather than just accurate classification. Furthermore, since the primary goal is to determine the number of devices to be misclassified, this approach uses a nonlinear programming problem to maximize the expected risk by minimizing misclassification costs. In conclusion, the proposed approach offers a realistic solution to the classification problem by incorporating risk, semi-SMART, and smart filtering techniques. In a system driven by an external agent, the concept of work is clearly defined. However, when a system evolves autonomously, driven by its internal dynamics, the notion of work is less clear-cut. Research has indicated that thermodynamic systems, trapped in a cycle of repeated dissipation, can be seen as being driven by an external agent, and a quantity called dissipated work makes sense in this context. Dissipated work is directly related to the internal work produced by the system as a whole from one state to another. Therefore, considering a system in a box, where transitions occur due to collisions with the wall, a new definition of work is proposed. Based on this definition, every system can be seen as being driven by an external agent, and a generalised notion of dissipated work is introduced. A crucial property of this work quantity is that it remains invariant under a change in variables. Moreover, when applied to a heat conductor, it yields the entropy of the system plus its effects on the outside world. Finally, when used to study thermodynamic systems in equilibrium, it yields the logarithm of the maximum work that could be produced in a limited time. All of these properties make the dissipated work a useful tool for the study of thermodynamic systems. In fact, when used in the study of a system with a single degree of freedom, it yields the Hertzian contact stiffness. When applied to gas systems, it accurately predicts the time to reach equilibrium. In addition, when used to study thermally driven systems, it yields the minimum change in temperature, and when used to study mechanically driven systems, it yields the minimum power. Therefore, the dissipated work offers a valuable general framework for the study and comparison of different thermodynamic systems. We analyze the participation ratio and spread of a two-level Markovian quantum walk on a circle with 251 sites, tracing its evolution back to the moment of 'detrapping'. Our findings reveal that as the initial trapping angle approaches the detrapping angle (~ 81 degrees), the participation ratio remains steady before suddenly dropping. Furthermore, the spread exhibits slow growth near the detrapping angle compared to its behavior further from it. Our research also shows that the participation ratio and spread are largely insensitive to the choice of driving angle but heavily rely on it for their initial exploration. We then delve into the long-term behavior of this model, demonstrating that the participation ratio and spread eventually level out and settle at fixed values that hinge on the initial trapping angle. To gain further insight, we dissect the quantum walk into its coherent and incoherent components, each of which exhibits intriguing patterns in the participation ratio and spread. Our work concludes by considering scenarios where the driving amplitude is adjusted rather than the driving angle, leading to interesting findings including the participation ratio and spread reaching a universal maximum (>0.9) at a particular amplitude on this particular setup. We then explore how these results might be applied to broader scenarios. All data discussed herein is presented in supplementary materials available online. We used NumPy to implement the quantum walk model described in Aragao et al., 2020. To visualize our data, we used Matplotlib. We also verify that our implementation of the quantum walk model adheres to its expected properties, namely that it remains unitary, conserves probability, and exhibits long-term behavior dominated by its largest eigenvalue. Additional details are provided in the supplementary materials available online. DINO, a self-supervised learning method, uses an unsupervised version of the popular Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture. By employing a self-distillation technique with multiple models, DINO achieves superior performance compared to other self-supervised and supervised methods on ImageNet. However, DINO's efficiency comes at the cost of significantly increasing the computational cost by a factor of 2.5-4 times for each benchmark we examined. This large gap in performance and complexity raises questions about the robustness of DINO's advantages. In this research, we address these two critical issues by first revealing that DINO's success is largely attributed to an uneven comparison with supervised methods that utilize extra resources (more models, datasets, and computations). We then extracted the key components of DINO and incorporated them into a conventional ViT model, resulting in a highly efficient self-supervised method called FeViT. FeViT uses a single model to achieve comparable performance with DINO on ImageNet while also reducing the computational cost by a factor of 2.5 times. We thoroughly tested FeViT on various benchmarks and found it to be a versatile and efficient self-supervised method. Additionally, we used FeViT to achieve impressive results on other datasets, including CIFAR-10/100, Tiny ImageNet, and Adience in challenging few-shot learning scenarios. Furthermore, we found that FeViT produces robust and interpretable features by analyzing its performance on various semantic segmentation benchmarks. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the exceptional value of self-supervised learning, in this case DINO, while also removing its drawbacks to yield a robust and efficient method, FeViT. We strongly believe that other researchers can learn from this work in the future. The proposed work is now available on https://github.com/stuartgj/FeViT. Building upon the user-guided image creation system known as Artist, we introduce Stable Artist, an iteration that enables users to seize artistic control by specifying desired outcomes through comparative references. By incorporating a key comparison clue, users can define tasks that Artist optimally completes, resulting in more precise control over the image generation process. The comparison clue is incorporated into the network by augmenting latent vectors, allowing the network to produce highly detailed images while maintaining its stability. The resulting advancements in comparison-based drawing, painting, and manipulation tasks demonstrate the power of cooperative human-machine systems, as validated by user evaluations. Furthermore, Stable Artist facilitates the creation of innovative tools, such as instance mapping, that leverage comparisons to produce accurate and fine-grained results. We visually illustrate these applications, showcasing Stable Artist's capacity to produce realistic and tailored outcomes. Stable Artist's source code and demonstration are publicly available at https://github.com/arthas2019/Stable-Artist.
